meta.blurb: A teacher sits on a hillside above the Sea of Galilee, and the crowd leans in. He calls the gentle and the peacemakers blessed, then speaks of anger, money, worry and trust. These are the words of Jesus in Matthew's Gospel.
meta.bible: The Sermon on the Mount: the longest teaching of Jesus, recorded in the Gospel of Matthew, chapters five to seven. Jesus: a teacher from Nazareth in Galilee, whom Christians follow as the Son of God. Matthew: the writer of the Gospel that records the sermon; Christian tradition names him as a former tax collector, though scholars debate who wrote it. Galilee: the region of northern Israel where Jesus taught. Sea of Galilee: the lake beside which the crowds gathered. Capernaum: a fishing town on the shore of the lake, near where tradition places the sermon. Disciples: the close followers of Jesus. Simon Peter, Andrew, James and John: four fishermen whom Jesus called to follow him. Decapolis: the Ten Towns, a group of cities east of the lake. Jerusalem, Judea and the Jordan: places the crowds came from. The Beatitudes: the opening blessings, each beginning Blessed are. Law and Prophets: the holy writings of the Jewish people in his day. Scribes and Pharisees: respected religious teachers of his day; the Gospels' picture of them is debated and must never be used against Jewish people today. Father: the name Jesus uses for God. Lord's Prayer: the prayer Jesus taught his followers, which begins Our Father. Solomon: the famous king of ancient Israel. Rome and Roman: the empire that ruled the land at the time. Heaven. Christians. Mammon: an old word for money and wealth. Gehenna: a valley outside Jerusalem used in Jesus' sayings as a picture of judgment. Moses and Mount Sinai: the lawgiver of Israel and the mountain where the Law was given. Luke: another Gospel, with a shorter teaching set on a level place. Didache: an early Christian teaching text. Augustine, Martin Luther, Tolstoy, Gandhi, Martin Luther King, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Albert Schweitzer: later readers of the sermon. Mennonites and Quakers: Christian groups. Lutherans. Psalm. Church of the Beatitudes. Confucius: Chinese teacher who lived about five hundred years before Jesus. Hillel: Jewish teacher who lived shortly before Jesus. Leo Tolstoy: Russian novelist; his book The Kingdom of God Is Within You. Mohandas Gandhi: Hindu leader of non-violent campaigns in South Africa and India. Martin Luther King: Baptist pastor in Montgomery, Alabama; his 1957 sermon Loving Your Enemies. Dietrich Bonhoeffer: German pastor; his 1937 book The Cost of Discipleship; Nazis, Germany. North Africa. Sermon on the Plain: Luke's shorter teaching. Egypt, Israel, Russia, India, South Africa. Baptist. Jewish. Pharisees. Voice and tone: calm, respectful and clear. Everything is attributed to Matthew's Gospel and to Christian tradition. Never preach, never criticise other faiths, never invent words for Jesus. Where a saying is understood in different ways, say so.

beats.scene: Green hills and fishing boats beside the Sea of Galilee
beats.summary: Galilee in Jesus' day is a green, crowded land beside a lake, ruled from far away by Rome.

beats.scene: Jesus walks between Galilean villages and teaches in a synagogue
beats.summary: Jesus travels from village to village, teaching in the synagogues and telling people good news about God's kingdom.

beats.scene: Four fishermen leave their nets on the shore to follow Jesus
beats.summary: Matthew's Gospel tells how Jesus called four fishermen, Simon Peter, Andrew, James and John, to follow him.

beats.scene: Sick people are carried on mats to Jesus
beats.summary: People bring the sick and suffering to Jesus, and Matthew says he healed them.

beats.scene: Travellers on dusty roads come toward Galilee from far and near
beats.summary: News of Jesus spreads, and crowds come from Galilee, the Ten Towns, Jerusalem, Judea and beyond the Jordan.

beats.scene: Farmers, mothers, fishermen and children stand together in the crowd
beats.summary: The crowd is made of ordinary people with ordinary hopes and worries, and many of them are poor.

beats.scene: Jesus climbs a grassy hillside above the lake with the crowd below
beats.summary: Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up a mountainside, which tradition places near Capernaum.

beats.scene: Jesus sits on the hillside while his disciples gather close
beats.summary: Jesus sits down, as a teacher of his day usually did, and his disciples come to him.

beats.scene: The crowd falls silent as Jesus opens his mouth to speak
beats.summary: The crowd grows quiet, and Jesus begins to teach.

beats.scene: Matthew writes the sermon on a scroll by lamplight
beats.summary: Matthew's Gospel records the sermon in three chapters, and the book now sets out what it holds.

beats.scene: A small group of people open their hands as Jesus begins to bless them
beats.summary: Jesus begins with blessings, and the word blessed can also be translated happy or fortunate.

beats.scene: Nine short blessings written in a row, each with a promise
beats.summary: The nine blessings, called the Beatitudes, each name a kind of person and then a promise.

beats.scene: A man with empty hands looks up at a bright sky
beats.summary: The first blessing is for the poor in spirit, who know how much they need God.

beats.scene: A rich man in fine clothes looks surprised as a poor man is blessed
beats.summary: The blessing surprises the crowd, because people usually honoured the rich and strong.

beats.scene: A woman in a dark shawl weeps beside a quiet grave
beats.summary: The second blessing is for those who mourn, who are promised comfort.

beats.scene: Two mourners hold one another under an olive tree
beats.summary: Readers understand mourning in different ways, as grief for loss and sorrow over wrong, and both receive comfort.

beats.scene: A gentle shepherd leads sheep over a quiet hill
beats.summary: The third blessing is for the meek, who are promised the earth.

beats.scene: A Roman soldier strides past a patient villager on the road
beats.summary: Meek does not mean weak, and Jesus praises the gentle at a time when Rome ruled by force.

beats.scene: A hungry child reaches for a small piece of bread
beats.summary: The fourth blessing is for those who hunger and thirst for what is right, who are promised they will be filled.

beats.scene: A woman at a well looks hopefully toward a distant city
beats.summary: Hunger was familiar to the poor, and Jesus speaks of a hunger for justice and goodness.

beats.scene: A man gives a loaf of bread to a hungry traveller
beats.summary: The fifth blessing is for the merciful, who are promised mercy.

beats.scene: Neighbours forgive a debt and clasp hands across a fence
beats.summary: Mercy shows in actions such as feeding the hungry and forgiving wrongs.

beats.scene: A child with clear eyes stands in a bright field
beats.summary: The sixth blessing is for the pure in heart, who are promised that they will see God.

beats.scene: A man puts down a mask and a heavy bag at a doorway
beats.summary: In the Bible the heart means the whole inner self, and purity means an honest and undivided life.

beats.scene: Two quarrelling neighbours shake hands while others look on
beats.summary: The seventh blessing is for the peacemakers, who will be called children of God.

beats.scene: A soldier of Rome stands guard over a market while villagers watch
beats.summary: Roman peace was kept by soldiers, but Jesus praises those who make peace by building bridges.

beats.scene: A man is led away by guards while a friend watches
beats.summary: The eighth blessing is for those who are persecuted for doing right, who are promised the kingdom of heaven.

beats.scene: Followers smile together although others point at them and shout
beats.summary: Jesus tells his followers to rejoice when they are insulted for following him, since their reward is great.

beats.scene: A line of ancient prophets walks along a dusty road
beats.summary: Jesus reminds them that the prophets before them were also treated badly, so they are in good company.

beats.scene: A teacher spreads nine blessings across a stone ledge like a portrait
beats.summary: The nine blessings together paint a picture of a person, and the first and the eighth share the same promise.

beats.scene: A cook holds a pinch of coarse salt over a clay pot
beats.summary: Jesus tells his followers, You are the salt of the earth.

beats.scene: Salt spread on fish to keep it fresh in the sun
beats.summary: In the ancient world salt gave flavour and kept food from spoiling.

beats.scene: Spilled salt that has lost its taste is trampled on a path
beats.summary: Salt that has lost its saltiness is useless and is thrown out and trampled.

beats.scene: A bright lamp shines in the dark window of a village house
beats.summary: Jesus tells his followers, You are the light of the world.

beats.scene: A hill town glowing with lamplight under the night sky
beats.summary: A town on a hill cannot be hidden, and its lights can be seen from far away.

beats.scene: A small clay lamp burns on a stand in a one-room house
beats.summary: People lit small oil lamps and set them on a stand so that the whole house could see.

beats.scene: A basket sits on the floor beside a lamp that is not covered
beats.summary: Nobody lights a lamp and then puts a basket over it.

beats.scene: Neighbours look at a woman's kind deeds and give thanks to heaven
beats.summary: Jesus says his followers should let their good deeds shine so that others praise the Father in heaven.

beats.scene: A lamp passes light to another lamp across a dark room
beats.summary: Good deeds are meant to point toward God and not toward the person who does them.

beats.scene: Salt and lamp side by side on a wooden table
beats.summary: Salt and light are only useful when they leave the jar and the lampstand, and they are for others.

beats.scene: Scrolls of the Law and the Prophets lie open on a rough table
beats.summary: The Law and the Prophets were the holy writings of the Jewish people, and Jesus' listeners knew them well.

beats.scene: Jesus raises a hand as the crowd listens closely
beats.summary: Jesus says he has not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfil them.

beats.scene: A scribe and a student bend over a half-written scroll
beats.summary: The word fulfil can mean to complete or to bring to full meaning, and readers explain it in different ways.

beats.scene: A scribe holds a reed pen over the smallest letter on a scroll
beats.summary: Jesus says that not the smallest letter will pass away until everything is accomplished.

beats.scene: A man teaches a child from an open scroll while an older man watches
beats.summary: Jesus says the one who keeps the commandments and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

beats.scene: A Pharisee in careful robes stands in the temple court
beats.summary: Scribes and Pharisees were respected teachers known for strict obedience, and the Gospels' picture of them is debated.

beats.scene: Jesus lifts a finger as a hush falls over the hill
beats.summary: Jesus says his followers' goodness must go deeper than that of the scribes and Pharisees.

beats.scene: Six stone tablets stand in a row on a hillside
beats.summary: Jesus now gives a series of six sayings, each beginning, You have heard that it was said, but I say to you.

beats.scene: Jesus speaks without a scroll while a scribe listens
beats.summary: Jesus teaches in his own name and does not simply quote earlier teachers.

beats.scene: A heart drawn on a scroll with a line for the law around it
beats.summary: A theme runs through the six sayings: goodness belongs in the heart and not only in actions.

beats.scene: A stone tablet reads Do not murder while a crowd of villagers nods
beats.summary: Jesus begins with the old command, You shall not murder, which all of his listeners knew.

beats.scene: An angry man shakes a fist at a quiet neighbour
beats.summary: Jesus says that anger toward a brother or sister is also serious.

beats.scene: A man shouts at his neighbour across a village street
beats.summary: Insults such as calling someone a fool are also serious, Jesus says, because they come from the same root.

beats.scene: A seed of anger sprouts into a bitter plant
beats.summary: The point is that violence begins in the heart, and so does peace.

beats.scene: A man with a lamb walks the road toward the temple in Jerusalem
beats.summary: People travelled to the temple in Jerusalem with gifts and offerings for God.

beats.scene: A man stops at the altar, and a friend stands far behind him
beats.summary: If you remember at the altar that someone has something against you, Jesus says, leave your gift.

beats.scene: A man hurries home down the road to make peace
beats.summary: First go and be reconciled with the other person, and then come and offer your gift.

beats.scene: Two men walk toward a courthouse on a dusty road
beats.summary: Agree quickly with your opponent while you are still on the way to court.

beats.scene: A judge and a guard stand over a man at the court
beats.summary: If you wait, you may end up before the judge, and the guard, and in prison.

beats.scene: A small flame of anger is put out with a jar of water
beats.summary: The lesson is practical: put out a quarrel before it becomes a fire.

beats.scene: A husband and wife stand beneath a wedding canopy
beats.summary: Jesus turns to faithfulness and recalls the commandment, You shall not commit adultery.

beats.scene: A man lowers his eyes and turns away from a woman in the street
beats.summary: Jesus says that looking at someone with lust is already a sin in the heart.

beats.scene: A man looks into a still pool at his own face
beats.summary: The teaching is about the inner life, since actions begin with what is in the mind.

beats.scene: A man covers one eye with a hand as he walks on
beats.summary: Jesus says that if your eye causes you to sin you should tear it out, a strong figure of speech.

beats.scene: A man holds up an open hand in front of a crowd
beats.summary: Jesus says the same of the hand, and readers have not usually taken these words literally.

beats.scene: A scribe writes a certificate of divorce at a table
beats.summary: In Jesus' day the Law allowed a man to divorce his wife with a written certificate.

beats.scene: A husband and wife sit together at a table with bread
beats.summary: Jesus says divorce except for unfaithfulness is wrong, and Christians today differ in how they apply this.

beats.scene: A woman stands alone at a door with a small bundle
beats.summary: A divorced woman could be left with nothing, and many readers think Jesus is protecting her.

beats.scene: A man lifts a hand to heaven as he makes a promise
beats.summary: The old law said not to swear falsely, but Jesus says do not swear at all.

beats.scene: Two friends shake hands and smile after speaking truthfully
beats.summary: Let your yes be yes and your no be no, because honest speech needs no oath.

beats.scene: A man weighs a stone against a stone on a scale
beats.summary: The old law said an eye for an eye, which limited revenge so that it could not grow without end.

beats.scene: A man looks calmly at the one who has just insulted him
beats.summary: Jesus says not to answer evil with evil.

beats.scene: A man offers his other cheek with a calm face
beats.summary: If someone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other, a way of refusing to return an insult.

beats.scene: A man lays a second garment on the table before a judge
beats.summary: If someone sues you for your shirt, give your coat as well.

beats.scene: A Roman soldier hands a pack to a villager on a dusty road
beats.summary: A Roman soldier could force a local person to carry a load for a mile, and Jesus says to go two.

beats.scene: A man gives a coin to a beggar and lends to a neighbour
beats.summary: Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow.

beats.scene: Gandhi sits beside King as both look at a tattered book
beats.summary: Readers such as Gandhi and Martin Luther King found in these sayings a pattern for non-violent resistance.

beats.scene: Christians in conversation, some holding a sword, some holding a dove
beats.summary: Christians differ on what the words mean for nations and defence, and many have held that they apply to personal conduct.

beats.scene: A chain of revenge is broken by a hand reaching out
beats.summary: The point is to break the chain of revenge by answering with generosity.

beats.scene: A man walks beside the soldier who has taken his bundle
beats.summary: The sayings share one idea: do more than is asked, and do not be ruled by revenge.

beats.scene: A neighbour and a stranger stand side by side
beats.summary: Jesus recalls the command to love your neighbour, which comes from the Law.

beats.scene: Jesus faces a crowd that includes Roman soldiers and tax collectors
beats.summary: But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.

beats.scene: Villagers watch a Roman soldier and a tax collector in the market
beats.summary: The enemies in the crowd have names and faces: a rival, a cheating neighbour, a tax collector, a Roman soldier.

beats.scene: A man prays quietly in a field at dusk
beats.summary: Praying for an enemy is where love begins, because it changes how you see that person.

beats.scene: A child looks up at a father who is smiling
beats.summary: Love of enemies marks you as a child of your Father in heaven.

beats.scene: Sun and rain fall on a field of wheat and a field of weeds
beats.summary: God makes the sun rise on the evil and the good and sends rain on the just and the unjust.

beats.scene: A tax collector counts his coins at a table
beats.summary: If you love only those who love you, what is the reward, since even tax collectors do the same?

beats.scene: Two friends greet each other in a market square
beats.summary: If you only greet your friends, you do no more than others do.

beats.scene: A crowd of listeners stares at a great circle drawn in the dust
beats.summary: Be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect, and the Greek word suggests being complete.

beats.scene: Six small stones arranged in a row beside a path
beats.summary: The six sayings together take in murder, adultery, divorce, oaths, revenge and enemies, each pointing to the heart.

beats.scene: Three paths branch from one road: a gift, a prayer, a fast
beats.summary: Jesus turns to three practices of Jewish life: giving to the poor, prayer and fasting.

beats.scene: A man stands in a market square watched by many people
beats.summary: Beware of doing good only to be seen by others.

beats.scene: A man blows a trumpet over a coin in a crowded market
beats.summary: When you give, do not announce it with trumpets, as the hypocrites do.

beats.scene: An actor in a mask bows to a clapping crowd
beats.summary: The word hypocrite meant an actor, and they have already received their reward in the applause.

beats.scene: Two hands, one hiding a coin from the other
beats.summary: Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.

beats.scene: A woman puts a coin into a poor man's hand
beats.summary: Giving to the poor was central to Jewish life, and Jesus asks that it be done quietly.

beats.scene: A quiet room with a closed door and a lamp
beats.summary: Your Father who sees in secret will reward you.

beats.scene: A man stands in a street corner and prays with a loud voice
beats.summary: When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites who love to pray where people can see.

beats.scene: A woman closes the door of a small room and kneels
beats.summary: Go into your room, close the door, and pray to your Father in secret.

beats.scene: A man babbles long, empty words while a woman prays simply
beats.summary: Do not heap up empty phrases, for your Father knows what you need before you ask.

beats.scene: Jesus holds out both hands and speaks gently to his followers
beats.summary: Jesus says to pray in this way and gives a short prayer that has become famous.

beats.scene: A child folds hands and looks up at the sky
beats.summary: The prayer begins, Our Father in heaven, and the word our joins every person who prays it.

beats.scene: Light on a hilltop as a voice sings praise
beats.summary: May your name be kept holy, the prayer says.

beats.scene: A field in morning sun with a road leading to a distant city
beats.summary: Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as in heaven.

beats.scene: A basket of fresh bread on a village table
beats.summary: Give us today our daily bread, a request for what we need for one day.

beats.scene: Two neighbours tear up a list of debts together
beats.summary: Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors, and some versions say trespasses or sins.

beats.scene: A traveller walks past a dark thicket toward a lit house
beats.summary: Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.

beats.scene: A scroll with a closing line added in a different hand
beats.summary: Many churches add the closing, For yours is the kingdom, which scholars say was added to later copies of the Gospel.

beats.scene: A man forgives a neighbour and a door opens for him
beats.summary: Right after the prayer Jesus says that if you forgive others, your Father will forgive you.

beats.scene: Christians in many countries say the same prayer in different languages
beats.summary: The prayer has been said every day for about two thousand years in nearly every language, and Luke's Gospel has a shorter version.

beats.scene: A man fasts and walks with a sad face and untidy hair
beats.summary: Jesus says that when you fast, do not look gloomy as the hypocrites do.

beats.scene: Worshippers gather at dawn without eating, each in quiet thought
beats.summary: Fasting was an old practice of the Jewish people, undertaken to show sorrow or to seek God.

beats.scene: A man washes his face and smooths oil on his hair
beats.summary: Anoint your head and wash your face, so that no one can tell you are fasting.

beats.scene: A moth eats a cloak beside rusting tools in a mud-brick house
beats.summary: Do not store up treasures on earth, where moths and rust destroy and thieves break in.

beats.scene: A thief digs through the wall of a mud-brick home
beats.summary: In a house of mud brick a thief could dig through the wall, so earthly treasure is never safe.

beats.scene: A chest of treasure glows in the clouds above a hill
beats.summary: Store up treasure in heaven, where nothing can destroy or steal it.

beats.scene: A merchant looks at a chest of gold as a lamp burns beside him
beats.summary: Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

beats.scene: An open eye lets light into a room; a closed eye sits in darkness
beats.summary: The eye is the lamp of the body: a healthy eye fills it with light, and a bad eye leaves it in darkness.

beats.scene: A servant stands between two masters who are pulling in opposite directions
beats.summary: No one can serve two masters, since he will love one and hate the other.

beats.scene: A man standing between a temple and a pile of coins
beats.summary: You cannot serve God and money, which the text calls Mammon.

beats.scene: A woman looks anxiously at an empty grain jar
beats.summary: Therefore, Jesus says, do not worry about your life, what you will eat or drink or wear.

beats.scene: A table with a loaf, a cup and a plain cloak
beats.summary: Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothes?

beats.scene: A flock of sparrows takes off from a wheat field
beats.summary: Look at the birds of the air, which do not sow or reap, yet the Father feeds them.

beats.scene: A small bird lands on a woman's hand
beats.summary: Are you not worth more than they are?

beats.scene: A man looks at his own shadow and shrugs
beats.summary: Can any of you add a single hour to your life by worrying?

beats.scene: Red poppies and white lilies bloom across a green hillside
beats.summary: Look at the wild flowers: they do not work or spin, yet they grow.

beats.scene: A king in gold robes stands beside a simple field flower
beats.summary: Not even Solomon in all his glory was dressed like one of these flowers.

beats.scene: Dry grass lies bundled beside a clay oven
beats.summary: If God clothes the grass that is burned tomorrow, how much more will he care for you?

beats.scene: A traveller on a road who does not stop to worry
beats.summary: Those who do not know God run after these things, but your Father knows what you need.

beats.scene: Dawn rises over the lake as a man walks calmly toward the day
beats.summary: Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and do not worry about tomorrow.

beats.scene: Two people face each other with scales in their hands
beats.summary: Jesus says, Do not judge, or you will be judged.

beats.scene: A measuring cup fills with grain for a neighbour
beats.summary: The measure you use on others will be used on you.

beats.scene: A balance holds two bowls of grain, one marked mercy
beats.summary: The measure you use echoes the prayer: we are forgiven in the same way we forgive others.

beats.scene: A woman looks at a friend with a gentle face
beats.summary: Jesus is warning against harsh and hypocritical judging, and not against all careful thought about right and wrong.

beats.scene: A man looks into his friend's eye while a speck floats there
beats.summary: Why do you look at the speck in your friend's eye and ignore the log in your own?

beats.scene: A carpenter in a workshop with a long plank in one eye
beats.summary: Matthew uses a humorous picture of someone with a plank in his eye offering to remove a speck.

beats.scene: A man takes a plank out of his own eye and sees clearly
beats.summary: First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to help your friend.

beats.scene: A scattered handful of pearls in a pigpen
beats.summary: Do not give what is holy to dogs or throw pearls to pigs.

beats.scene: A man thinks quietly, his hands full of pearls
beats.summary: Readers explain this saying in different ways, but many say it asks for wisdom about what to share and with whom.

beats.scene: A man bows his head and looks at himself
beats.summary: Judging with humility links back to the blessing for the poor in spirit.

beats.scene: A closed door and an open door side by side
beats.summary: Jesus has told his followers to trust God, and now he shows how to ask.

beats.scene: A boy knocks on a door and it opens
beats.summary: Ask and it will be given to you, seek and you will find, and knock and the door will be opened.

beats.scene: A woman asks for bread and receives a loaf
beats.summary: Everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds.

beats.scene: A father hands a loaf of bread to his son
beats.summary: Which of you, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone?

beats.scene: A father hands a fish to a smiling child
beats.summary: If he asks for a fish, will you give him a snake?

beats.scene: A parent gives a gift to a happy child
beats.summary: If you, who are not perfect, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will God?

beats.scene: A man helps a woman lift a load beside a road
beats.summary: So in everything, do to others what you would have them do to you.

beats.scene: Scrolls of the Law and the Prophets bound with a ribbon
beats.summary: Jesus says this sums up the Law and the Prophets, and it is often called the Golden Rule.

beats.scene: Teachers of different lands each hold a scroll with a similar saying
beats.summary: Similar sayings appear in other traditions, but Jesus states it as an action to take.

beats.scene: A child gives half of her bread to a hungry boy
beats.summary: The rule asks us to act for others, and not only to avoid harming them.

beats.scene: A narrow gate stands in a stone wall beside a wide arch
beats.summary: Enter through the narrow gate, for the gate is wide and the road easy that leads to destruction.

beats.scene: A crowd streams through a wide road under a bright arch
beats.summary: Many are on the broad road, and many enter by that gate.

beats.scene: A single traveller climbs a narrow path up a hill
beats.summary: The gate to life is narrow and the road is hard, and only a few find it.

beats.scene: Two paths split in a green valley under a bright sky
beats.summary: The picture of two ways was familiar from Psalm 1 and from Moses' call to choose life.

beats.scene: A man stands at a fork and looks at both ways
beats.summary: The choice is real, and the few does not tell us who is on which road.

beats.scene: A wolf in a sheep's fleece walks among the sheep
beats.summary: Beware of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but are wolves inside.

beats.scene: A gardener examines fruit on a tree
beats.summary: You will know them by their fruit.

beats.scene: A gardener looks at a thornbush and a vine
beats.summary: Do people pick grapes from thorn bushes or figs from thistles?

beats.scene: A woodcutter swings an axe at a tree with no fruit
beats.summary: A good tree bears good fruit and a bad tree bad fruit, and a tree that bears none is cut down.

beats.scene: A tree heavy with ripe fruit beside a gate
beats.summary: By their fruit you will recognise them, so look at what a person does.

beats.scene: A man bows and says Lord, Lord with an empty heart
beats.summary: Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven.

beats.scene: A farmer works in a field while his neighbour watches
beats.summary: Only the one who does the will of my Father enters.

beats.scene: A crowd stands before a throne of light
beats.summary: On that day many will say, Lord, did we not prophesy and do wonders in your name?

beats.scene: Jesus turns away from a man who knelt before him
beats.summary: Jesus will answer, I never knew you, and Christians read this serious saying in different ways.

beats.scene: A man holds up his own good deeds as a shield
beats.summary: Words, titles and even impressive deeds are no substitute for a life of obedience from the heart.

beats.scene: A builder digs down to bedrock and lays a stone foundation
beats.summary: Anyone who hears these words and acts on them is like a wise man who built on rock.

beats.scene: Rain, flood and wind beat against a house on rock
beats.summary: The rain fell, the floods rose, and the winds blew, and the house stood.

beats.scene: A dry riverbed in Galilee fills quickly with water
beats.summary: In Galilee a dry stream bed could fill with a sudden flood after rain.

A1A2: Galilee was a green land beside a big lake, and Rome ruled it.
Jesus walked from town to town and taught in the meeting places.
By the lake, Jesus called four fishermen, and they left their nets to follow him.
People brought their sick friends to Jesus, and he made them well.
News about Jesus spread, and people came from many places to see him.
In the crowd were farmers, fishermen, mothers and children, and many were poor.
Jesus saw the crowd, so he walked up a hill beside the lake.
Jesus sat down on the hill, and his friends came close to him.
The people became quiet, and Jesus began to teach them.
Matthew wrote down this teaching, and we can still read his words today.
Jesus began with the word blessed, which can also mean happy.
Jesus gave a list of blessings, and each one has a promise.
Jesus said that people who know they need God are blessed.
The crowd was surprised, because people thought rich and strong people were blessed.
Jesus said that people who are very sad will be comforted.
Some people are sad about loss, and some are sad about wrong things.
Jesus said that gentle people are blessed, and they will have the earth.
Gentle does not mean weak, and Rome did not value gentle people.
Jesus said that people who want to do right will be filled.
Poor people knew hunger well, so they understood these words about wanting what is right.
Jesus said that people who show mercy to others will receive mercy.
Mercy means feeding hungry people and forgiving people who have done wrong.
Jesus said that people with a pure heart will see God.
In the Bible, the heart means your whole inner self, and pure means honest.
Jesus said that people who make peace are blessed, and God will call them his children.
Rome kept peace with soldiers, but Jesus praised people who make peace in other ways.
Jesus said that people who suffer for doing right are blessed too.
He told his followers to be glad when people say bad things about them.
He reminded them that people treated the old prophets badly too.
The first and last blessings share one promise: the kingdom of heaven.
Jesus told his followers that they are like salt for the world.
In those days, people used salt to give food taste and keep it fresh.
Salt that has lost its taste is no good, so people throw it away.
Jesus also told them, “You are the light of the world.”
A town on a hill cannot hide, and people can see its lights.
People used small clay lamps, and they put them up high in the house.
Nobody lights a lamp and then puts a basket over it.
Jesus said that good deeds should shine, so people will praise God.
Good deeds should make people look toward God, and not toward us.
Salt and light are only useful when they help other people.
The Law and the Prophets were the holy books of the Jewish people.
Jesus said, “I did not come to end the Law, but to complete it.”
People explain the word complete in different ways, but all agree it is not an ending.
Jesus said that not even the smallest letter of the Law will pass away.
He said that people who obey the commands and teach them will be called great.
Scribes and Pharisees were teachers who tried very hard to obey every rule.
Jesus said that his followers must be better than the scribes and Pharisees.
Next, Jesus gave six sayings, and each one started with the words “You have heard.”
Jesus spoke with his own authority, and he did not just repeat old teachers.
In each saying, Jesus asks for goodness in the heart and not only in actions.
Jesus began with the old command, “You shall not murder,” which everyone knew.
Jesus said that being angry with a brother or sister is serious too.
He said that calling a person a fool is also serious.
Anger starts in the heart, and so does peace.
People travelled to the temple in Jerusalem with gifts for God.
Jesus said, if you remember at the altar that someone is angry with you, stop.
First go and make peace with that person, and then bring your gift.
If someone has a case against you, agree with him quickly on the way to court.
If you wait, the judge may send you to a guard and then to prison.
The lesson is clear: stop a quarrel quickly, before it grows too big.
Jesus next spoke about marriage, and about keeping a promise to your husband or wife.
He said that wanting someone who belongs to another person is wrong in the heart.
The teaching is about the heart, because every action starts with a thought.
Jesus said, “If your eye makes you do wrong, take it out.”
He said the same about the hand, but people do not take this word for word.
In those days, a man could end his marriage with a written paper.
Jesus said that ending a marriage is wrong, and churches today understand this in different ways.
A divorced woman could be left with nothing, so Jesus may have wanted to protect her.
The old law said not to swear falsely, but Jesus said not to swear at all.
He said, “Let your yes be yes and your no be no.”
The old law said “an eye for an eye,” so revenge could not grow bigger.
Jesus said, “Do not answer evil with evil.”
If someone hits you on the cheek, turn your other cheek to him.
If someone takes your shirt, give him your coat as well.
A Roman soldier could make you carry his bag for one mile.
Jesus said to carry it two miles, and to give to people who ask.
Gandhi and Martin Luther King found a way of peaceful protest in these sayings.
Christians do not all agree about what these words mean for countries and armies.
The idea is to stop revenge by answering with kindness.
These sayings share one idea: do more than people ask, and do not take revenge.
The Law told people to love their neighbour, and many also hated their enemies.
But Jesus said, “Love your enemies, and pray for people who hurt you.”
An enemy could be a bad neighbour, a rival, or a Roman soldier.
Praying for an enemy changes how you see that person.
Love like this shows that you are a child of your Father in heaven.
God lets the sun shine and the rain fall on good and bad people.
Jesus said that if you only love people who love you, that is not special.
If you only greet your friends, you do no more than other people.
Jesus said, “Be perfect, as your Father in heaven is perfect.”
Now the six sayings were finished, and each one pointed to the heart.
Jesus now spoke about three things: giving to the poor, prayer, and fasting.
He said, “Be careful not to do good only so that people see you.”
When you give, do not blow a trumpet, as some people do.
The word actor was used for people who do good only to be admired.
Jesus said, “Do not let your left hand know what your right hand does.”
Giving to poor people was very important in Jewish life, and Jesus asked for quiet giving.
Your Father sees what you do in secret, and he will reward you.
Do not pray loudly on street corners so that everyone can see you.
Go into your room, shut the door, and pray to your Father.
Do not use many empty words, because your Father knows what you need.
Jesus said, “Pray like this,” and he gave his followers a short prayer.
The prayer begins, “Our Father in heaven,” and the word our joins everyone.
Next it says, “May your name be kept holy,” and holy means very special.
Then it says, “Your kingdom come, and your will be done on earth.”
The prayer asks, “Give us today the bread that we need.”
It asks God to forgive us as we forgive other people.
It asks God not to let us fall into trouble, and to keep us from evil.
Later, many churches added a last line about God's kingdom, power and glory.
After the prayer, Jesus said that if you forgive people, God will forgive you.
People have said this prayer for about two thousand years, in many languages.
Jesus said, “When you fast, do not look sad, as some people do.”
Fasting means going without food for a time, to show sorrow or to pray.
He said to wash your face and put oil on your hair.
Jesus said, “Do not save up treasure on earth, where moths and rust destroy it.”
Many houses were made of mud bricks, so a thief could dig through the wall.
Save your treasure in heaven, where nothing can destroy it or steal it.
Jesus said, “Where your treasure is, your heart will be there too.”
He said that the eye is the lamp of the body.
If your eye is bad, your whole body is full of darkness.
No one can serve two masters, God and money, so you must choose.
Jesus said, “Do not worry about what you will eat or drink or wear.”
He asked, “Is life not more than food, and the body more than clothes?”
Jesus said, “The birds do not plant seeds, yet your Father feeds them.”
He asked, “Are you not worth much more than the birds?”
Worrying cannot add even one hour to your life, Jesus said.
Flowers do not work or make clothes, yet they grow, Jesus said.
Not even King Solomon was dressed as beautifully as one of these flowers.
God dresses the grass of the field, so he will surely care for you.
Other people run after food and clothes, but your Father knows what you need.
He said, “Look for God's kingdom first, and do not worry about tomorrow.”
Jesus said, “Do not judge other people, or you will be judged.”
He said, “The measure you use will be used on you.”
This is like the prayer, where God forgives us as we forgive others.
Jesus does not mean we should never think about right and wrong.
He asked, “Why do you see dust in your friend's eye?”
But you do not see the big piece of wood in your own eye.
First take the wood from your own eye, then you will see clearly.
Jesus said, “Do not give what is holy to dogs, or pearls to pigs.”
People explain this saying in different ways, and it asks us to be wise.
To judge well, we must first see our own weakness and be humble.
Jesus had told them to trust God, and now he taught them how to ask.
Jesus said, “Ask, seek and knock, and God will answer you.”
Everyone who asks receives, and everyone who seeks finds, Jesus said.
He asked, “If your son asks for bread, will you give him a stone?”
He asked, “If he asks for a fish, will you give him a snake?”
Parents are not perfect, but they know how to give good gifts.
Jesus said, “Do to others what you want them to do to you.”
Jesus said this sums up the Law, and people call it the Golden Rule.
Other teachers in other lands have taught something like this rule too.
This rule asks us to do good for others, not only to avoid harm.
Jesus said, “Go in through the narrow gate, not the wide gate.”
Many people go through the wide gate, but it leads to ruin.
The narrow road leads to life, but only a few find it.
The picture of two roads was an old one in the Bible.
The choice is real, but we cannot tell who is on which road.
Jesus said, “Be careful of false teachers, who look like sheep but are wolves.”
He said, “You will know them by their fruit.”
People do not pick grapes from thorn bushes or figs from weeds.
A good tree gives good fruit, and a bad tree is cut down.
So look at what a person does, not only at what he says.
Jesus said that words alone are not enough to enter God's kingdom.
Only people who do what the Father wants will enter his kingdom.
On that day many will say they did great things in his name.
Jesus said he will answer, “I never knew you,” a serious saying.
Words, titles and even great deeds do not replace a heart that obeys.
Whoever hears these words and does them is like a wise builder.
He built his house on rock, so it stood in rain, flood and wind.
In Galilee a dry stream bed could fill quickly with a flood after rain.
Whoever hears these words and does not act is like a foolish builder.
The foolish man built on sand, and his house fell with a great crash.
When Jesus finished speaking, the crowd was amazed.
They were amazed because he taught as a man with authority.
Other teachers quoted older teachers, but Jesus said, “I say to you.”
Matthew put the teaching of Jesus into five great parts.
Some readers see Jesus as a new Moses teaching on a mountain.
In short, Jesus spoke about blessing, light, the heart, trust and building well.
Matthew says Jesus taught his followers while the crowd listened too.
Matthew wrote for early Christians, to help them remember what Jesus taught.
A church marks the old place, but no one knows the exact spot.
The sermon's pictures were so simple that people could repeat them at home.
Luke's Gospel has a shorter teaching like this, given on level ground.
Readers explain the differences in several ways, and some say Jesus taught often.
A very old Christian book, the Didache, uses words from the sermon.
Around the year 394, Augustine wrote a book about the sermon.
Martin Luther preached on the sermon and said it was for everyone.
Leo Tolstoy, a Russian writer, read the sermon as a call for peace.
Gandhi, a Hindu, said the sermon went straight to his heart.
In 1957 Martin Luther King preached a sermon called Loving Your Enemies.
In 1937 Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a German pastor, wrote a book on the sermon.
Some Jewish readers admire the sermon and see it as part of Jewish teaching.
Christians read the hard sayings in several different ways.
Some groups, such as Mennonites and Quakers, try to follow the sermon closely.
Others, including many Lutherans, say it shows how much we need grace.
Many read it as a guide for the heart, not as strict rules.
Albert Schweitzer thought Jesus expected God's kingdom to come very soon, but others disagree.
The sermon moves from who we are to what we do.
Its pictures come from daily life: salt, lamps, birds, flowers, gates and houses.

People of every background have asked what kind of person they want to be.
When Jesus came down the mountain, crowds followed, and his words are still read.
B1B2: In the time of Jesus, Galilee was a green and crowded land beside a large lake. It was part of the Roman Empire, and many families found life hard.
Jesus travelled from village to village, teaching in the synagogues and telling people the good news of God's kingdom. Matthew says that he did this all over Galilee.

One day, as he walked beside the lake, Jesus saw two brothers, Simon Peter and Andrew, casting a net. He called them to follow him, and soon James and John, another pair of brothers, left their boat and their father to follow him too.
Wherever Jesus went, people brought him those who were sick or in pain. Matthew says that he healed them, and this made more and more people want to see him.
News about Jesus travelled quickly along the roads of Galilee and beyond. Matthew lists the places that the crowds came from: Galilee, the Ten Towns, Jerusalem, Judea and the land across the Jordan.
The crowd was made up of ordinary people, such as farmers, fishermen, mothers and children. Many of them were poor, and most had worries about food, health and the future.
When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up a mountainside, which tradition places near the town of Capernaum. The slopes beside the lake would have made a natural place to speak to so many people.
Jesus sat down, which was the usual way for a teacher to teach in his day. His disciples came and gathered close around him, and the rest of the crowd listened from behind.
The noise of the crowd faded away until the whole hillside was quiet. Then Jesus opened his mouth and began to teach, and Matthew records what he said.
Matthew's Gospel records the sermon in three chapters, which are chapters five to seven. Christian tradition names Matthew as a former tax collector, although scholars debate who wrote the Gospel.
Jesus began the sermon with a series of blessings. The word blessed can also be translated happy or fortunate, and it describes people who are in a good place with God.
The blessings are usually counted as eight or nine, and each has the same pattern. First it names a kind of person, and then it makes a promise to that person.
The first blessing is for the poor in spirit, which means those who know how much they need God. Jesus says that the kingdom of heaven belongs to them.

This blessing must have surprised the crowd, who were not used to hearing such things. In that time most people admired the wealthy and the strong, and few would have said that those with empty hands were fortunate.
The second blessing is for those who mourn, and Jesus promises that they will be comforted. Most families in the crowd had buried someone they loved, so they knew what these words meant.
Readers understand the word mourn in more than one way. Some think of grief after a death, while others think of sorrow over the wrong in the world, and the promise of comfort fits both.
The third blessing is for the meek, and Jesus says that they will inherit the earth. The saying echoes a line from Psalm 37, a song that the crowd would have known.

The word meek can sound weak in English, but it means gentle and humble, with strength held under control. Jesus said this when the Roman army ruled the land by force, which made his words even more daring.

The fourth blessing is for those who hunger and thirst for what is right, and Jesus promises that they will be filled. He is describing people who want goodness as much as a hungry person wants bread.
Hunger was a real and familiar thing for many poor families in the crowd. When Jesus spoke of hungering for justice and goodness, he chose a picture that everyone understood.
The fifth blessing is for the merciful, and Jesus promises that they will receive mercy. It is a simple idea: those who show kindness to others will find kindness shown to them.
Mercy is more than a feeling, because it shows itself in actions. It can mean feeding someone who is hungry, forgiving someone who has done wrong, or helping a person who cannot repay you.
The sixth blessing is for the pure in heart, and Jesus promises that they will see God. Only those with nothing to hide, he suggests, can look toward God without fear.

In the Bible the heart is not only the place of feeling but the whole inner self, including thought and will. To be pure in heart is therefore to be honest and undivided, rather than merely clean on the outside.
The seventh blessing is for the peacemakers, who will be called children of God. Notice that Jesus does not praise those who simply enjoy peace, but those who work to make it.

The peace of Rome was famous, but it was kept by soldiers and was often paid for by the people it ruled. Jesus praises a different kind of peace, one that is built when people mend quarrels and refuse to hate.

The eighth blessing is for those who are persecuted for doing what is right, and Jesus again promises the kingdom of heaven. This does not mean that suffering is good in itself, but that those who stand firm in goodness are not forgotten.

Jesus then turns to his followers directly and says that they are blessed when people insult them and speak evil against them because of him. They should rejoice and be glad, he says, because their reward in heaven is great.

He also reminds them that the prophets before them were treated in just the same way. This means they are following in the footsteps of a long line of people who spoke the truth, and are in good company.

Taken together, the blessings paint a picture of a person who is humble, gentle, merciful, honest and peaceful. The first and the eighth blessing make the same promise, the kingdom of heaven, as if the whole list were wrapped inside it.
Jesus told his followers, “You are the salt of the earth.” He was not speaking to the crowd in general, but to those who had come close to be his disciples.
In the ancient world salt was very valuable to ordinary families. It gave flavour to plain food, and in a land without refrigerators it also kept fish and meat from going bad.
Jesus warned that salt which has lost its saltiness is useless. It is thrown out and walked on, because nothing can be done with it.
Then he said to the same listeners, “You are the light of the world.” In a village at night a single lamp could change a dark room into a place where people could see and work.
He pointed to a familiar sight in the hills of Galilee, a town built on a hilltop. At night its lights could be seen from a great distance, and there was no way to hide them.
Most people lit small clay lamps filled with olive oil, and a family's whole house was often a single room. A lamp was placed on a stand so that everyone could benefit from its light.
Jesus asked a question to which the answer was obvious. Nobody lights a lamp and then covers it with a basket, because that would defeat the whole purpose of lighting it.
His followers, he said, should let their light shine in front of others. Then people would see their good deeds and give praise to their Father in heaven.
Notice carefully where the praise is meant to go in this saying. The good deeds are meant to point people toward God and not toward the person who does them, which is a hard thing to remember.
Salt and light are alike in one way: neither is any use if it stays in the jar or under the basket. Jesus is telling his followers that their lives are meant to be given away for the good of others.
The Law and the Prophets were the holy writings of the Jewish people. Jesus' listeners had heard them read aloud in the synagogue since they were children, and some knew whole passages by heart.
Jesus told the crowd that he had not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. Instead, he said, he had come to fulfil them and bring them to their full meaning.
The word fulfil can mean to complete, or to bring something to its full meaning. Readers explain it in different ways, but nearly all agree that Jesus is not sweeping the old teaching away.
Jesus said that until heaven and earth pass away, not the smallest letter of the Law will disappear. It was a striking way to show how seriously he took the holy writings.
He added that anyone who ignores even the least commandment and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom. Anyone who keeps them and teaches them will be called great.

The scribes and the Pharisees were respected teachers of the Law, known for obeying its rules carefully. The Gospels' picture of them is debated, and it should never be used to judge Jewish people today.
Then Jesus said something that must have shocked the crowd: their goodness must go deeper than that of the scribes and Pharisees. Otherwise, he said, they would not enter the kingdom of heaven.
Jesus now gave a series of six sayings that follow a pattern. Each begins with the words, “You have heard that it was said,” and goes on with the words, “But I say to you.”
This second phrase is very important to the meaning of the sermon. The scribes usually quoted the opinions of earlier teachers, but Jesus spoke in his own name, as if he had the right to do so.
There is also a theme that runs through all six of the sayings. Jesus keeps moving the question from what a person does on the outside to what is happening inside the heart.
Jesus began the first of his six sayings with a command that everyone in the crowd knew. “You shall not murder,” the Law said, and no one on the hillside would have disagreed.
But Jesus went further than the old command did, and his next words were a surprise. He said that anyone who is angry with a brother or sister will be answerable for it, just as a murderer would be.

He gave an example: whoever insults another person, or calls them a fool, is also in danger. In Matthew's words the penalty rises step by step, from a local judge to the council to the fire of Gehenna.
The point is that violence begins in the heart. Murder is only the last step on a road that starts with a cruel thought and a bitter word.
Jesus then gave a picture from daily religious life. Many people travelled to the temple in Jerusalem, carrying an animal or another gift to offer to God.
Imagine, he said, that you are standing at the altar when you suddenly remember that someone has something against you. You should leave your gift there in front of the altar.
Go first and make peace with that person, Jesus said, and only then come back to offer your gift. In other words, making peace with a neighbour is not something that can wait until worship is over.
He also gave practical advice about what to do when someone takes you to court. If someone has a case against you, agree with him quickly while you are still on the way to court.
If you do not, he warned, you may be handed to the judge and then to the guard, and end up in prison. Jesus wanted his listeners to see how quickly a small dispute can grow into a serious one.
The lesson is a practical one, which is to put out a quarrel before it becomes a fire. Whoever acts at once to make peace saves both sides a great deal of trouble.
Jesus turned to marriage and faithfulness, and he began with a command from the Law: “You shall not commit adultery.” This was the second of the sayings that begin with the words, “You have heard.”
But I say to you, Jesus continued, that anyone who looks at a woman with lust has already been unfaithful to her in his heart. He moves the question from what a person does to what a person wants.
The teaching is about the inner life, and the way that thoughts shape us. A person who never breaks a promise in public may still be nursing a desire that will one day grow into an action.
Jesus then used a strong figure of speech: if your right eye causes you to do wrong, he said, tear it out. It is better, he said, to lose one part of the body than the whole of it.

He said the same of the right hand, which should be cut off if it leads a person into wrong. Christian readers have not usually taken these words literally, since Jesus is using exaggeration to show how serious the matter is.
Jesus also spoke about the difficult subject of divorce. In his day the Law allowed a man to end a marriage by giving his wife a written certificate, and the matter was widely debated.

Jesus said that anyone who divorces his wife, except for unfaithfulness, does wrong. Christian traditions today differ in how they understand and apply this saying, and many also look at other Gospel passages.
In those times a divorced woman could be left with no home and no means of support. Many readers think that Jesus was speaking up to protect the person with the least power in the marriage.
The next saying was about the swearing of oaths, which was common. The old teaching said that you must not swear falsely, but must keep the promises that you make to the Lord.

But Jesus said not to swear oaths at all, whether by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem or even by your own head. Let your yes be yes and your no be no, he said, because honest people have no need of oaths to be believed.
Jesus now gave the fifth saying, which began with a famous rule: “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.” In its time this rule limited revenge, so that no one could take more than he had lost.
But I say to you, Jesus continued, do not resist an evil person. He did not mean that evil should be ignored, but that it should not be answered with more of the same.

Jesus said, “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well.” Many scholars think that such a slap was more an insult than an injury, so Jesus is describing a refusal to return an insult.
Jesus gave another example, and it was about a lawsuit. If someone sues you for your shirt, he said, give him your coat too, though a poor person's coat was often his only blanket.
The next example is probably about the Roman army. A soldier could force a local person to carry his pack for a mile, and Jesus said that you should go with him for two.
He also told his followers to give to everyone who asks and not to turn away from anyone who wishes to borrow. The saying asks for generosity that is wider than most people feel comfortable with.

Many people have found in these sayings a way of resisting wrong without using violence. The Hindu leader Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King, a Christian pastor, both said that the sayings shaped their ideas about peaceful protest.

Christians do not all agree about what these words mean for nations and their armies. Some think that they apply to all of life, while others think that they teach how an individual should treat other people.
Whatever one's view, one meaning is very clear to every reader. Revenge feeds on revenge, and a person who answers with generosity can break the chain.

The sayings share a single idea: do more than you are asked, and do not let others decide how you behave. In each of the pictures, the person who is wronged keeps the freedom to choose a better answer.
Jesus came to the sixth saying, and it began with a command that his listeners knew well. The Law told them to love their neighbour, and many of them added that they could hate their enemy.
But I say to you, Jesus told them, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you. It was perhaps the most surprising thing that he had said so far.
Who were the enemies of the people in the crowd? They might be a rival in the village, a thief who had robbed them, a tax collector, or a Roman soldier stationed nearby.
Prayer, Jesus suggests, is where love for an enemy begins. It is difficult to go on hating a person when you are asking God to bless him.
Love of this kind, he says, shows that you are children of your Father in heaven. You become like the one who gave you life, and you share his habit of giving to people who have not earned it.
Jesus gave a picture from nature to show what that habit looks like. God makes the sun rise on evil people and good people alike, and he sends the rain on the honest and the dishonest.
If you only love those who love you, Jesus asked, what reward is there in that? Even the tax collectors, who were widely disliked, do the same thing.
And if you only greet your own friends, what more are you doing than anyone else? Even people who do not know God do that much.
Jesus ended this section with a very high standard: be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect. The Greek word can also mean complete or whole, and it suggests love that has no gaps in it.
This is the sixth saying, and it brings the series to a close. Murder, adultery, divorce, oaths, revenge and enemies were each taken from the Law and each turned toward the heart.
Jesus now turned to three practices that were central to Jewish life: giving to the poor, prayer and fasting. For each of them he gave the same kind of warning.
Be careful, he said, not to practise your goodness in front of other people in order to be seen by them. If you do, you have no reward from your Father in heaven.

So when you give to the poor, he said, do not sound a trumpet in front of you, as the hypocrites do. Scholars debate whether this describes a real custom or is simply a joke, but the meaning is clear.

The word hypocrite comes from a Greek word for an actor, someone who plays a part on a stage. Those who give in order to be admired, Jesus said, have already received their reward in full, and the reward is the applause.
But when you give, he went on, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing. It is a funny picture that means giving should be so natural and quiet that you hardly notice it yourself.

Giving to the poor was one of the most important duties of the Jewish faith, and the Law told people to care for the needy. Jesus did not change this, but he asked that it should be done with a pure heart.

Your giving should be done in secret, Jesus said, and your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you. The reward is left in God's hands, and it is not something to be counted on or hurried.
He then spoke about prayer, which was the second practice. When you pray, he said, do not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray on street corners where everyone can see them.
When you pray, go into your room and close the door, and pray to your Father who is unseen. The words suggest that prayer is not a performance, but a quiet conversation between a person and God.

Jesus also said that you should not heap up empty phrases, as people do who think that they will be heard for their many words. Your Father knows what you need before you ask him, he said, and so prayer can be simple and honest.
Jesus said, “Pray then in this way,” and he gave his followers a short prayer. It has only a few lines, but it has become one of the most famous prayers in the world.
The prayer begins with the words “Our Father in heaven,” and the word our joins everyone who prays it. Jesus invites his followers to speak to God as a child speaks to a loving parent.
The first request is that God's name be kept holy. To hallow a name means to treat it as special, so the prayer asks that God be honoured everywhere.

Next the prayer asks that God's kingdom come and that his will be done on earth as it is in heaven. The one who prays is hoping for a world in which goodness rules, and is offering to take part in it.
Then comes a simple request: give us today our daily bread. Bread was the food that most poor families lived on, and the request is for what is needed for one day.

The prayer goes on, “Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.” Different versions say trespasses or sins in place of debts, but all of them link our forgiveness from God with our forgiveness of others.

The last requests are for protection: do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil. The final word can also be translated the evil one, and it asks for help in the struggles that every person faces.

Many churches finish the prayer with the words, “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory for ever.” Scholars say that these words are not in the oldest copies of Matthew's Gospel, but were added by later copyists.
After the prayer Jesus returned to one of its lines. If you forgive others when they wrong you, he said, your Father will forgive you, but if you do not, neither will he forgive you.

Christians have said this prayer for about two thousand years, and they say it in nearly every language on earth. The Gospel of Luke records a shorter version, so different churches use slightly different words today.
Fasting was the third practice that Jesus spoke about. When you fast, he said, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, who make their faces look miserable so that people will notice.

Fasting simply means going without food for a period of time, as many people still do. In Jewish life it was a way of showing sorrow, asking forgiveness or seeking God, and some people fasted on set days of the year.
Instead, Jesus said, put oil on your head and wash your face, so that no one will know you are fasting. Your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you.

Then Jesus turned from prayer and fasting to the subject of wealth and possessions. He said that his followers should not store up treasure on earth, where moths and rust destroy it and thieves can break in.
Many Galilean houses were built of mud bricks, so a thief could dig through a wall. Even a locked door could not keep out a determined robber, and clothes and grain could be spoiled by insects.
Store up your treasure in heaven instead, Jesus said, where moths and rust cannot destroy and thieves cannot break in. He is speaking of what lasts, such as kindness, mercy and faithfulness.
Jesus gave a short reason: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. In other words, we tend to follow what we value, so it is wise to ask what our hearts are really set upon.
Jesus continued with another picture, saying that the eye is the lamp of the body. A healthy eye fills the whole body with light, but a bad eye leaves it in darkness.
Some scholars say that a good eye could mean a generous person, and a bad eye a greedy one. If this is right, then Jesus is saying that how we look at money shapes the whole of our lives.

Jesus then said that no one can serve two masters, because he will hate one and love the other. You cannot serve God and money, he said, and the word that he used for money is Mammon, an old word for wealth.
Next Jesus turned to a problem that every listener knew, which was worry about the needs of daily life. Do not worry about your life, he said, about what you will eat or drink or what you will wear.
For most of the people on the hillside, these were not idle worries. Many of them were poor, and a bad harvest or a lost day's work could mean a hungry family.
Look at the birds of the air, Jesus said, because they do not sow or reap or store grain in barns. Yet your heavenly Father feeds them, and Jesus wants his listeners to notice this simple fact.

Are you not much more valuable than they are, Jesus asked, if even the birds are fed by your Father? Jesus is not telling people to stop working, since the birds themselves must search for their food.
Can any of you add a single hour to your life by worrying? The point is that worry cannot lengthen life, and it can easily spoil the hours that we do have.
Then Jesus asked why his listeners worried so much about what they would wear each day. Look at the wild flowers, he said, which do not work or spin, and yet they grow.
Not even King Solomon in all his splendour was dressed like one of these flowers. Solomon was remembered as the richest and wisest king of Israel, so the comparison would have surprised the crowd.
If God clothes the grass, which is here today and burned tomorrow, will he not clothe you? Dry grass was often used as fuel in clay ovens, so the picture was a familiar one.
People who do not know God, Jesus said, spend their lives running after these things. Your heavenly Father knows that you need them, so you can trust him.
Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, Jesus said, and all these things will be given to you as well. So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself.
Jesus next spoke about a habit that is very common, which is judging the faults of other people. Do not judge, he said, or you will be judged, and the warning was meant for everyone in the crowd.
The measure you use on other people, Jesus said, will be used on you. In the market a seller measured out grain with a cup, and every buyer wanted a fair measure.
This saying echoes the Lord's Prayer, which asks God to forgive us as we forgive others. Those who are harsh with others can hardly expect gentleness for themselves.
Jesus is warning against the harsh and proud kind of judging that looks down on other people. He is not saying that we should never think carefully about what is right and wrong.
Then Jesus asked a question that may have made some people smile. Why do you look at the speck in your friend's eye, he said, and not notice the log in your own?
In the Greek, the word for the large thing is a beam of wood, the kind that holds up a roof. The picture is clearly meant to be funny, because nobody could really walk around with a beam in his eye.

First take the log out of your own eye, Jesus said, and then you will see clearly enough to help your friend. The aim is not to leave the friend's problem alone, but to help in a way that is honest and humble.
Jesus then gave a puzzling saying, which was that you should not give what is holy to dogs. Nor should you throw your pearls in front of pigs, or they may trample them and turn on you.

Dogs and pigs were unclean animals to many Jewish listeners, and a pearl was a very costly treasure. Readers explain the saying in different ways, but many say that it asks for wisdom about what to share and with whom.

Taken together, these sayings about judging call for a humble heart, one that is honest about its own failings. This links back to the first blessing for the poor in spirit, who know how much they need God.
Jesus had already told his followers to trust God with their daily needs. Now he turned to the subject of prayer once more and taught them to ask with confidence.
Ask and it will be given to you, Jesus said, and seek and you will find. Then he added a third picture, saying, knock and the door will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives, Jesus said, and the one who looks for something will find it. Many readers notice that the three verbs grow in effort, so they take this as a call to keep praying.
Which of you, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Jesus chose a picture from family life that every parent in the crowd could understand.
Or if he asks for a fish, will you give him a snake? Bread and fish were common meals beside the lake, and a round stone could look a little like a loaf.

If you, who are not perfect, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father give? The Greek word is stronger than not perfect, since it means evil, but Jesus is making a comparison and not a charge.
So in everything, Jesus said, do to others what you would have them do to you. It follows from the picture of a generous Father, since those who receive good things are asked to share them.
Jesus added that this one saying sums up the Law and the Prophets, the holy writings of his people. Because it is so short and so clear, it has long been called the Golden Rule.
Similar sayings appear in other traditions, including Jewish teaching and the sayings of Confucius in China. Some of them are put as warnings, while Jesus states the rule as something to do.
The rule asks us to act for others, and not only to avoid harming them. It is not enough to keep our hands clean if we leave a hungry neighbour with nothing.
Jesus now began to bring his teaching to a close with pictures of two gates and two roads. Enter through the narrow gate, he said, for the gate is wide and the road is easy that leads to destruction.
Many people are on that broad road, Jesus said, and many enter through the wide gate. It is easy to follow the crowd, because a broad road asks for no special effort.
But the gate to life is narrow and the road is hard, and only a few find it. A narrow path takes care and attention, because a traveller must watch every step.
The picture of two ways was familiar to Jesus's listeners from their own holy writings. The first Psalm speaks of two ways, and Moses asked the people of Israel to choose life instead of death.
The choice is real, but the word few does not tell us who is on which road. Jesus is not pointing at anyone here, and judging others would go against his earlier words.
Beware of false prophets, Jesus said, who come to you in sheep's clothing but are wolves inside. A prophet speaks for God, so a false prophet is a teacher who only claims to do so.
Wolves in sheep's clothing look just like the real flock, so how can anyone tell them apart? You will know them by their fruit, Jesus said, and fruit is something that anyone can see.
Do people pick grapes from thorn bushes, Jesus asked, or figs from thistles? Grapes and figs were two of the best-known fruits of the land, and a thorny plant cannot produce either.
A good tree bears good fruit, and a bad tree bears bad fruit. A tree that bears no good fruit at all is cut down and thrown into the fire.
By their fruit you will recognise them, Jesus repeated, and the fruit of a life is what it produces for others. So we are asked to look at what a person does over time, and not only at what he says.
Jesus now gave a serious warning about words that are not backed by actions. Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, he said, will enter the kingdom of heaven.
Only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven will enter. Jesus puts the weight on doing, and not only on saying the right words.
On that day many will say to me, Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name? Did we not drive out evil spirits and do many wonders in your name?
Then I will tell them plainly, Jesus said, I never knew you. Christians read this serious saying in different ways, but many see in it a warning to be sincere.
Words, titles and even impressive deeds are no substitute for a life of obedience. What matters most, the sermon suggests, is a heart that truly listens and then acts on what it has heard.
Jesus ended the sermon with a short story about two builders who each had to build a house. Anyone who hears these words of mine and acts on them, he said, is like a wise man who built on rock.
The rain fell, the floods rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house. Yet it did not fall, because it had its foundation on the rock.
In Galilee a dry stream bed could fill quickly with a sudden flood after rain. A house built beside such a stream needed a firm base, or the water would wash it away.
Everyone who hears these words and does not act on them, Jesus said, is like a foolish man who built on sand. Sand may look like good ground in dry weather, but it cannot hold a house in a storm.
Then the same storm came, with the same rain, the same floods and the same winds. That house fell with a great crash, and the story ends there.
When Jesus had finished saying these things, the crowds who had listened were amazed at his teaching. Matthew ends the sermon with a short note about how the listeners felt.
They were astonished because he taught as one who had authority of his own. He did not teach like their scribes, who were the usual teachers of the day.
Scribes in those days usually supported their words by quoting the opinions of earlier teachers. Jesus said, I say to you, and he spoke as if the words came from himself.

Matthew's Gospel arranges much of the teaching of Jesus into five great sections, and the sermon is the first. Each section ends with a similar phrase, such as when Jesus had finished saying these things.
Some readers see Jesus as a new Moses, who gives teaching from a mountain. Others read the scene more simply, as a teacher who goes up a hill so that the crowd can hear him.
In brief, the sermon spoke of blessings, light, a deeper law, secret devotion, trust, gentleness and building well. This brief list can help a reader to find the way through a long and rich teaching.
Matthew says that his disciples came to Jesus and he began to teach them. The crowd listened too, so readers ask who the sermon was really for.
Christian tradition says that Matthew wrote this Gospel for early Christians, probably many of them Jewish. He wanted them to remember what Jesus taught and to put it into practice.

Above the Sea of Galilee stands a church called the Church of the Beatitudes, which marks the traditional site of the sermon. Nobody knows the exact spot, and the Gospel only says that Jesus went up a mountainside.
The pictures of the sermon were so plain that ordinary listeners could remember them. A fisherman or a farmer could repeat them to his family at home beside the lamp.
Luke's Gospel has a shorter teaching that begins with blessings and is set on a level place instead of a mountainside. It also has warnings that match the blessings, which Matthew does not have.
Believers and scholars explain the differences between the two versions in several ways. Some say that Jesus taught the same things many times, and others that each writer shaped what he received.

A very early Christian writing called the Didache, probably from within a century of Jesus, uses the teaching of the sermon. It tells readers to pray for their enemies, to turn the other cheek and to give to anyone who asks.
In about 394 Augustine, a church leader in North Africa, wrote a long commentary on the sermon. He treated it as a map of the Christian life from the first blessing to the house on the rock.
In the 1500s Martin Luther preached through the sermon to the people of his town. He said that its teaching was for ordinary Christians as well as for monks.
In the 1800s the Russian writer Leo Tolstoy read the sermon as a command to non-violence. He wrote about it in a famous book called The Kingdom of God Is Within You.
Gandhi, who was a Hindu, wrote that the Sermon on the Mount went straight to his heart. He drew on its teaching in his campaigns of non-violent protest in South Africa and India.

In 1957 Martin Luther King preached a sermon called Loving Your Enemies, which was based on the words of Jesus. King, a Baptist pastor, taught that love and not hatred must guide the struggle for civil rights.

In 1937 the German pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer published a book about the sermon called The Cost of Discipleship. He warned against what he called cheap grace, which is forgiveness without any change of life.

Some Jewish readers admire the ethics of the sermon and see it as part of Jewish tradition. They may still differ with Christians about who Jesus was, and the sermon is a place where readers of both faiths can talk.

The hard sayings, such as turn the other cheek or tear out your eye, have been read in several different ways. Christians understand them differently, so it helps to know which readers hold which view.
Some groups, such as the Mennonites and the Quakers, try to follow the sermon quite literally. They have often refused to fight in wars and to swear oaths, because Jesus said, do not swear at all.
Others, including many Lutherans, say that the sermon shows how far we fall short of God's way. In their view it points us to our need for grace, because no one can keep all of it.
