Many other readers see the sermon as a direction for the heart and for character. They do not read it as a set of rules, but as a picture of the kind of person to become.

Albert Schweitzer, a scholar who wrote in the early 1900s, argued that Jesus expected God's kingdom to come very soon. He thought that Jesus taught for that short time, but other scholars dispute this view.
The sermon moves from who we are, in the blessings, to what we do. It ends with a call to act, in the story of the two builders.

The pictures of the sermon come from the everyday world, from salt, lamps, birds, wild flowers, gates and houses. These were things that every listener could see and touch, so the teaching was easy to carry home.

The sermon opens with a blessing for the poor and the gentle before it gives any command at all. Many readers see this as the key, since it suggests that people are welcomed before they are asked to change.

Readers of every background, believers or not, have taken the sermon as a question about what kind of person to be. Its pictures and sayings invite each one to think about mercy, honesty, peace and trust.
When Jesus came down from the mountainside, Matthew says, large crowds followed him. His words are still read today, and people of many faiths and none turn to them to ask how to live.
C1C2: When Matthew's Gospel opens its account of the sermon, the scene is Galilee, a green and crowded corner of the Roman world, where fishing villages hugged the shore of a large freshwater lake. Its people paid taxes to local rulers who answered to Rome, and they lived within sight of Roman power. For many families life was a daily struggle for bread, and this was the audience that Jesus was about to address.

Before the sermon, Matthew tells us, Jesus had been travelling from village to village, teaching in the synagogues and proclaiming the good news of God's kingdom. A synagogue was the local meeting place where Jewish communities gathered to pray and to hear the holy writings read aloud. It was a natural stage for a teacher who wished to be heard by ordinary people.

Matthew describes how, beside the lake, Jesus met two fishermen, Simon Peter and his brother Andrew, who were casting a net into the water. He invited them to follow him, and they left their nets at once, as did two more brothers, James and John, who abandoned their boat and their father. These four became the first of his disciples, and they would have been close by on the hillside.

Wherever Jesus went, the sick and the suffering were carried or led to him, and Matthew says that he healed them. Such stories travelled faster than any messenger, passing from market to market and from house to house. Before long, people who had never seen him were making plans to travel and hear him for themselves.

Matthew names the places that the crowds came from, and the list shows how far his reputation had spread: Galilee, the Ten Towns on the far side of the lake, Jerusalem, Judea and the land beyond the Jordan. Some had walked for days along dusty roads, carrying their children and their sick, and they had brought their questions with them. The sermon would therefore be heard by people from many villages and of many different backgrounds.

It is worth picturing who stood in that crowd: farmers who had left their fields, fishermen with salt-stiffened hands, mothers with babies on their hips, and old people who had waited a lifetime for a word of hope. Most were poor, and many had good reason to be anxious about food, health and the future. Their worries are important, because much of what Jesus said that day speaks directly to them.

Seeing the crowds, Jesus climbed a mountainside, and tradition places the spot near Capernaum, a fishing town on the northern shore of the lake. The word mountain may be generous, since the land there rises in gentle, grassy slopes that tumble down to the water. Nobody knows the exact place, but the setting would have carried a speaker's voice well to the crowd below.

Jesus sat down, which was the customary posture of a teacher in his day, and his disciples came and gathered around him. The rest of the crowd pressed in behind them, straining to catch every word. There was no stage, no scroll in his hand and no microphone, only a voice and an attentive hillside.

Matthew says simply that Jesus opened his mouth and began to teach, and the phrase carries a sense of solemn expectation. The murmur of the crowd died away, and even the children are likely to have fallen quiet. What followed would be remembered, copied and read aloud in homes and churches for many centuries to come.

The sermon fills three chapters of Matthew's Gospel, chapters five to seven, and it has become one of the best-known pieces of teaching in the world. Christian tradition names Matthew as a former tax collector who became one of the twelve disciples, though scholars still debate who wrote the Gospel and how the sermon was assembled. In this book the sermon is told in the order that Matthew gives it, with a few notes on how its words have been understood.

Jesus opened the sermon not with a command or a warning but with a blessing, and this choice sets the tone for everything that follows. The word translated blessed can also mean happy or fortunate, and it describes someone who is in a good place before God. These are the words that Christians call the Beatitudes, from a Latin word meaning blessed.

The Beatitudes are usually counted as eight or nine, depending on how the last ones are divided, and each follows the same simple pattern. A kind of person is named, and then a promise is made, sometimes about the future and sometimes about the present. Taken together they read like a portrait of a way of life that few would have chosen but that Jesus calls blessed.

The first blessing is for the poor in spirit, those who have no illusion of being self-sufficient and who know how much they depend on God. To them, Jesus says, belongs the kingdom of heaven, a promise that no wealth or status could ever buy. It is a surprising start, because it honours not the confident or the proud but those who come with empty hands.

His listeners were used to a world in which blessing seemed to follow money, health and power, and the poor were often assumed to have done something to deserve their poverty. By beginning as he did, Jesus overturned that assumption in a single sentence, and he did so in front of a crowd that included many of the poor. The shock was probably part of the purpose, since it made the crowd listen more closely.

The second blessing is for those who mourn, and the promise is that they will be comforted. In an age without modern medicine, many families on that hillside had buried a child, a parent or a friend, and grief was never far away. Jesus does not tell them that their sorrow is small, but he promises that it will not have the last word, and that comfort will follow.

Readers have understood mourning in more than one way, and the text allows for both. Some hear it as grief for those we have lost, while others hear it as sorrow over the wrongs and sufferings of the world, or over our own failings. Either way, the promise is that comfort will come to those who feel the weight of things.

The third blessing is for the meek, who will inherit the earth, and here Jesus echoes Psalm 37, a song that his listeners knew well and that also promises the land to the humble. The picture is of gentle people, long overlooked, finally receiving what the proud had grasped for. It is a promise that turns the usual order of power and pride completely upside down.

In English the word meek often suggests weakness, but the idea in the original text is closer to gentleness, humility and strength kept firmly under control. Jesus spoke these words while the Roman army held the land by force, and the ruling powers admired hardness above all. To praise the gentle in such a place was a quiet but daring act.

The fourth blessing is for those who hunger and thirst for what is right, and the promise is that they will be filled. The image is chosen with care, since it describes a longing as deep and as physical as the need for bread and water. Jesus is speaking of a hunger for justice, for goodness and for a world set right.

Hunger was no figure of speech for the poor in the crowd, many of whom knew what it was to go to bed with little to eat. To such people the picture of a longing that would one day be satisfied was powerful and kind. It also suggests that wanting goodness is itself something to be honoured, and not a weakness to be ashamed of.

The fifth blessing is for the merciful, and the promise is that mercy will be shown to them. The saying has a pleasing symmetry, as though kindness given were a seed that returns as kindness received. It is also a warning that a hard heart toward others will find the world, and perhaps God, equally hard in return.

Mercy in the Bible is never merely an inward feeling, since it always turns itself into deeds. It can be a loaf given to a hungry traveller, a debt cancelled for a neighbour, or a wrong forgiven when revenge would be easier. Jesus treats such acts as marks of someone who has understood what God is like.

The sixth blessing is for the pure in heart, and the promise is that they will see God. For the crowd on that hillside, seeing God was the deepest hope of a devout life, and here it is offered not to the powerful or the learned but to those whose hearts are clean. The sentence asks every listener to consider honestly what lies beneath a good reputation and a respectable name.

In the Bible the heart is not simply the seat of emotion but the centre of the whole person, where thought, desire and will come together. To be pure in heart is therefore to be honest and undivided, with inner motives that match outward actions. It means more than ritual cleanliness, since it concerns the person who stands behind the washing.

The seventh blessing is for the peacemakers, who will be called children of God, and the choice of word matters. Jesus does not bless those who merely love a quiet life, or who avoid conflict, but those who take the trouble to repair what has been broken between people. Such work is costly, and the promise that it brings a place in God's family is a high honour.

Every listener knew the Roman peace, a calm kept by legions and roads and heavy taxes, and many of them had paid for it. Against that background, Jesus praises a different way of making peace, one that is built by patience, forgiveness and a refusal to return hatred for hatred. The contrast would have been plain to every listener without a single further word of explanation from Jesus.

The eighth blessing is for those who are persecuted because they stand for what is right, and again the promise is the kingdom of heaven. Jesus does not claim that suffering is good in itself, only that those who endure it for the sake of goodness are neither forgotten nor defeated. It was a comfort to a crowd that knew very well how costly honesty could be.

Turning from the general to the personal, Jesus tells his followers that they are blessed when others insult them, persecute them and speak lies about them because of him. They are to rejoice and be glad, he says, because their reward in heaven is great. It is a remarkable instruction, and it is given not as a threat but as an encouragement.

He reminds them that the prophets before them were treated in exactly the same way, with insults, rejection and sometimes worse. Those who suffer for the truth are therefore not strangers in history but members of a long and honourable line. The thought must have given courage to followers who were afraid of what might lie ahead.

Read together, the blessings sketch a portrait of a person who is humble, gentle, hungry for justice, merciful, honest and peaceful, and willing to pay a price for it. It is worth noticing that the first blessing and the eighth make the very same promise, the kingdom of heaven, as though the whole list were held inside a single frame. The remainder of the sermon will go on to say what such a life looks like.

“You are the salt of the earth,” Jesus said to his followers, and the picture would have been plain to anyone who cooked or kept food. Notice that he did not say they should try to become salt, or that they might be someday, but that they already were. His words were addressed to the disciples who had gathered round him, though the crowd was listening too.

Salt in the ancient world was precious, since it gave flavour to dull meals and, in a land without refrigeration, it also preserved fish and meat from rotting. To call someone salt was to say that they were useful, even essential, in the life of those around them. The people of Galilee, who salted their catch from the lake, knew exactly what that meant.

But salt that has lost its saltiness, Jesus warned, is good for nothing and is simply thrown out to be trampled underfoot. Some scholars point out that the salt of the time was often impure, so that its taste could wash away and leave only a useless powder. The warning is that followers who lose their distinctive quality have lost the very thing that made them valuable.

In the next breath he changed the picture and said, “You are the light of the world.” In a village at night, one small flame could turn a dark and frightening room into a place where people could see, eat and work. Light, like salt, exists for the benefit of others, and it fulfils its purpose only when it is seen.

Jesus then pointed to a sight that his listeners knew from the hills around them: a town built on a height, which could not be hidden. After dark its scattered lamps would glitter for miles across the valley, and travellers would steer by them. The image suggests that the life of his followers would be visible whether they wished it or not.

The lamp of those days was a small clay vessel filled with olive oil, with a wick that burned with a modest flame, and in most homes a single lamp served a whole one-room house. It was therefore set on a stand, high enough that its light could fall on everyone inside. To put it anywhere else would have been a waste of precious oil, and no household could afford to waste it.

Jesus asked a question to which no answer was needed, since nobody lights a lamp and then hides it under a basket. The whole purpose of lighting it is to give light, and covering it would defeat that purpose entirely. His point was clear: a faith kept completely hidden has stopped doing what faith is for.

His followers, he said, should let their light shine before others, so that people may see their good deeds and give praise to their Father in heaven. The word is not that they should show off but that their deeds should be so good that onlookers are drawn to think of God. It is a gentle instruction and a demanding one, both at the same time, and it sets the tone for much that follows.

There is a subtle point in the final words, because the praise is meant to travel past the doer and arrive at God. Good deeds that call attention to the person who performs them have missed their target, while good deeds that lift the eyes of others have hit it. Jesus will return to this very point later in the sermon, when he speaks about giving, prayer and fasting.

Salt and light have something in common: neither does any good while it stays in the jar or under the basket, and both are useful only when they are spent on others. Jesus presents the life of a disciple in exactly that way, as something given away for the good of the world. With these two pictures the opening section of the sermon draws to its close.

When Jesus finished speaking about salt and light, he turned to the holy writings of his people, which his listeners called the Law and the Prophets. These included the five books of Moses and the later messages of the prophets, and the crowd had heard them read aloud in the synagogue since childhood. Some of them could probably have recited whole chapters from memory, line by line, without a scroll in front of them.

Jesus assured them that he had not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them. The remark appears to answer a worry that a radical new teacher might sweep away everything they cherished. He is saying, rather, that he stands inside the story of his people and not outside it.

The word fulfil has been read in more than one way, and the difference between those ways really does matter. It may mean to complete or bring to its goal, to show the full meaning of what was written, or to obey it perfectly, and thoughtful readers have defended each. What nearly all agree on is that Jesus does not describe himself as a destroyer.

Jesus said that until heaven and earth pass away, not the smallest letter or the tiniest stroke of a pen will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished. The image is a vivid one, since it picks out the tiny marks that distinguish one Hebrew letter from another. It is a way of showing how seriously he took the holy writings, and how much he wanted his listeners to take them seriously too.

He went on to say that anyone who relaxes even one of the least of the commandments, and teaches others to do the same, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Whoever keeps them and teaches them, by contrast, will be called great in that kingdom, and the saying is meant to be taken seriously. The saying places a high value on both doing and teaching, and it gives no support at all to careless obedience of any kind.

The scribes and the Pharisees were the teachers whom ordinary people looked up to, men who studied the Law in detail and tried to obey it with great care. The Gospels often present them as opponents of Jesus, but historians debate how fair that picture is. It should never be used as a reason to think badly of Jewish people today, or of anyone else.

Then came the sentence that must have startled everyone, in which Jesus told his followers that their righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees. If they did not, he said, they would never enter the kingdom of heaven. How could anyone be more careful than those who spent their lives on careful obedience?

The answer begins with the next section, in which Jesus gives a series of six sayings that all follow the same pattern. Each opens with the words, “You have heard that it was said,” and each turns on the words, “But I say to you.” The sayings deal in turn with murder, adultery, divorce, oaths, revenge and the way we treat our enemies.

Notice the boldness in that second phrase, because the scribes of the day usually backed their teaching by quoting famous teachers who had come before them. Jesus did not cite an earlier rabbi, but spoke in his own name, as one who had the right to explain what the Law was really for. The crowd would soon remark on it, as Matthew tells us at the end of the sermon.

A single idea runs through all six sayings, and it explains what Jesus meant about a deeper righteousness. Again and again he moves the question from what a person does on the outside to what is happening in the heart, where actions begin. A person who has never struck anyone may still be full of anger, and it is that hidden anger that Jesus wants to address.

Jesus began the first of his six sayings with a command that every listener knew by heart: “You shall not murder.” It was one of the oldest and most respected rules in the Law of Moses, and no one on the hillside would have argued with it. But Jesus, who said that he had come to bring the Law to its full meaning, was not content to leave the matter there.

Anyone who is angry with a brother or sister, he said, will be answerable for it, just as the murderer is. It is a startling comparison, since it seems to put a flash of temper on the same scale as a killing. Yet the point is not that the two are equal but that both come from the same root.

He went on to give examples of the way that anger grows, naming the insult and the contemptuous word, such as calling someone a fool. In Matthew's account the penalty climbs by steps, from a local court to the council to the fire of Gehenna. Gehenna was a valley outside Jerusalem, and in these sayings it works as a picture of final judgment.

Jesus is not trying to frighten his listeners with these words, but to show how seriously he takes the damage that hatred can do. Violence does not begin with the fist or the knife, he suggests, but with a cruel thought and a bitter word. If those are checked early, then the worst deeds may never happen, and the peace of a whole village may be saved.

Next he drew a vivid picture from the religious life of the time, one that every listener could easily imagine. Many people made long journeys to the temple in Jerusalem, carrying an animal, grain or another offering to present to God at the altar. For a devout person it was one of the most solemn acts of the year.

Imagine, said Jesus, that you are standing at the altar, with your gift in your hands, when you suddenly remember that a brother or sister has something against you. In such a moment, he says, you must leave your gift right there in front of the altar. The scene is deliberately startling, because nobody in their right mind would interrupt such a sacred act for any reason at all.

Go first and make peace with that person, Jesus says, and only afterwards come back and offer your gift to God. The meaning is plain, even if the image is dramatic: reconciliation with a neighbour is not an optional extra that can wait until the worship is finished. Our relationships with each other and with God, Jesus is saying, are bound up together and cannot easily be pulled apart.

Jesus then turned to another picture, this time from the law courts, which were familiar to many people in his audience. If someone has a case against you, he advised, settle it quickly with that person while you are still on the way to court. The advice is the sort that any sensible person could follow, and it needs no special holiness.

If you do not, he warned, your opponent may hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the officer, and you may be thrown into prison, where you will stay until you have paid the last penny. The picture is of a small matter that grows into a disaster through delay. Pride and stubbornness, he suggests, always carry a high price, and delay only makes that price larger.

The practical lesson of the whole section is that a quarrel should be dealt with while it is still small, before it spreads like fire. Jesus wants his followers to be quick to apologise and quick to forgive, and to see that this work of repair is as sacred as any ceremony. It is a theme that returns a little later in the sermon, in the words of the Lord's Prayer, where forgiveness is again at the centre.

Jesus now turned to faithfulness in marriage, and he began once more with the voice of the Law: “You shall not commit adultery.” This was the second of the six sayings, and like the first it was a rule that no one in the crowd would have questioned. Marriage was the foundation of family life, and breaking its promises caused great harm.

But I say to you, Jesus continued, that anyone who looks at a woman with lust has already been unfaithful to her in his heart. In a single sentence he moves the question from the visible act to the secret desire that comes before it. The sentence is demanding, and it was meant to be, since it exposes how little a purely outward goodness can achieve.

The teaching is really about the inner life, and about the way in which a wrong action grows from a seed planted much earlier. A man who has never broken a promise in public may still be cherishing a longing that will one day bear fruit. Jesus asks his listeners to look carefully at what they feed in their own minds.

He then used one of the sharpest figures of speech in the whole sermon. If your right eye causes you to stumble, he said, tear it out and throw it away, since it is better to lose one part of the body than to have the whole body thrown into Gehenna. Nobody in the crowd could have missed the shock of such a picture, and it has stayed in the memory of readers ever since.

The same was said of the right hand, which should be cut off if it leads a person into wrong. Christian readers have almost never taken these words literally, and they have pointed out that exaggeration was a common way of teaching in the lands of the Bible. Jesus is saying, in the strongest language available, that nothing is worth more than a clean conscience and a faithful heart.

Jesus then spoke about divorce, which was a very live question among the teachers and the families of his day. The Law allowed a man to end his marriage by giving his wife a written certificate, but teachers disagreed about the grounds on which it could be done. Some allowed it for almost any reason at all, while others permitted it only in a few serious cases.

Jesus said that anyone who divorces his wife, except in the case of unfaithfulness, does wrong. Christian traditions today differ in how they understand this teaching, and many also look at other places in the Gospels that discuss marriage. It is a subject on which sincere readers have reached more than one conclusion.

It helps to remember how life was arranged in that time, when a divorced woman could be left without a home or any means of support. Many readers think that Jesus was speaking up for the person with the least power in the marriage, who could be sent away at will. If so, then the saying is meant as a protection for the weak, and not simply as a rule that makes life harder.

The next saying concerned oaths, which were common in daily life, and it began with the old teaching that a person must not swear falsely but must keep the vows made to the Lord. People often swore by heaven, by the earth or by the holy city, to make their words sound more solid. There was a danger that a promise sworn by something grand might be taken more seriously than a plain promise spoken honestly.

But Jesus told them not to swear at all, whether by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem or by their own heads. His alternative was beautifully simple: let your yes be yes and your no be no. A person who always speaks the truth, he implies, has no need of oaths to be believed.

Jesus now gave the fifth of his six sayings, and it began with a famous rule from the Law of Moses: “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.” In its own time that rule was a restraint, since it meant that revenge could not exceed the injury and could not spread without limit. It was a principle of fair and proportionate justice in a harsh and often violent world.

But I say to you, Jesus continued, do not resist an evil person, and the words have puzzled and challenged readers ever since. He cannot have meant that evil should be ignored or accepted, since the whole sermon calls for goodness, but that it should not be met with the same weapon. The saying asks for a different and much harder kind of strength than the one the world admires.

Jesus said, “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well.” Many scholars think that a blow on the right cheek, given with the back of the hand, was a way of insulting someone rather than of causing serious injury. If so, then Jesus is describing a calm refusal to repay an insult in kind, and not a weak surrender.

Jesus gave a second example from the law courts: if someone takes you to court to claim your shirt, he said, give him your coat as well. A poor man's coat was often his only blanket on a cold night, and the Law said that it must be returned by sunset. To give it freely would therefore show, with real force, how little you cared for the quarrel.

A third example probably comes from the daily presence of the Roman army, because a soldier had the right to force a local person to carry his pack for a mile. People resented this bitterly, and yet they had no choice in the matter, since refusing could bring a harsh punishment. Jesus told his followers to go with the soldier for two miles, which turned an act of force into an act of free generosity.

He then told his followers to give to anyone who asks, and not to turn away from the person who wants to borrow. This is a demanding standard, and it reaches far beyond what most people feel comfortable doing. The saying does not remove the need for wisdom, but it leaves no room for a closed hand.

Many people in later centuries have found in these sayings the seed of a way to resist wrong without using violence. Mahatma Gandhi, who was a Hindu, and Martin Luther King, a Christian pastor, both said that the sayings helped to shape their ideas about peaceful protest. Their campaigns, which cost them dearly, showed how much determination and courage such a path can demand.

Christians have not all agreed about what the words mean for nations and their armies. Some hold that they must govern every part of life, including public life, while others believe that they teach how an individual should treat those who do wrong to him. Honest readers have argued about the difference for centuries, and the discussion is far from over.

What can be said with confidence is that revenge feeds on itself, since each blow calls for another, and the cycle can turn for generations. A person who answers with generosity breaks that cycle at the point where it is easiest to continue it. The result is that one person, at least, is no longer controlled by the wrongdoer.

All of these sayings share a single idea, which is to do more than you are asked and to refuse to let another person decide how you behave. In every picture the wronged person keeps the freedom to choose a better answer, and by choosing it he takes back some power. It is a very different view of strength from the one the world usually admires.

The sixth saying began with a command that every listener knew: love your neighbour. That commandment comes from the Law of Moses, but to it many people had added a second half, that they might hate their enemy. Jesus did not accept the addition, and what he said instead is among the most demanding sentences in all of Jesus' teaching.

Love your enemies, Jesus said to the crowd, and pray for those who persecute you and make your lives harder. These words ask for a kind of goodness that goes well beyond fairness, and they apply to the people whom it is hardest to forgive. If the crowd had been expecting a gentle sermon, they were certainly now being challenged.

The enemies of the people on that hillside were not abstract, since they had names and faces and often lived nearby. One was a rival who had cheated them in the market, another a neighbour who insulted their family, a third a tax collector who took too much, and a fourth a Roman soldier who treated them with contempt. Jesus was asking for a love that could survive real hurts, the kind that do not fade after a night's sleep.

Prayer is where he begins, since it is nearly impossible to go on hating someone whom you are asking God to bless. Praying for an enemy does not mean pretending that the wrong was small, but it does change the way the person is seen. A face that was once a target becomes the face of someone God loves.

Such love, Jesus says, shows that his followers are children of their Father in heaven. They become like the one who gave them life, and they share his habit of giving to those who have not earned it. In this way the command is not a burden added to nature, but an invitation to take on the family likeness.

He gave a picture of that habit from the world around them: God makes the sun rise on evil and good alike, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous. A farmer could not ask for rain on his own field alone, and the sky made no distinctions. If God's generosity has no favourites, then the generosity of his children should not have any favourites either, whatever the cost.

If you love only those who love you, Jesus asked, what reward do you deserve? Even the tax collectors, whom most people despised and avoided, do as much as that for their own friends and families. The question exposes how ordinary and unremarkable it is to be kind only to those who are kind to us.

And if you greet only your own friends and family, he continued, what are you doing more than other people? Even those who do not know God behave in the same way, since affection for one's own circle comes naturally to nearly everyone. The test of real love is what it does for the stranger, the rival and the person who is unkind to us.

The section closes with a very high standard: be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect. The word translated perfect can also mean complete or whole, and many readers take it to describe a love that has no gaps in it and does not stop at a boundary. The sentence is an aim to be followed for a lifetime, not an examination to be passed in a day.

With these words the series of six sayings comes to an end, and a pattern is plain. Murder, adultery, divorce, oaths, revenge and enemies were each taken from the Law and each turned toward the heart, where the real source of conduct lies. In every case Jesus shows that the deepest goodness is not just keeping the rules but becoming a certain kind of person.

Jesus now turned from the law of the heart to the life of devotion, and he chose three practices that stood at the centre of Jewish religious life: giving to the poor, prayer and fasting. For each of these he offered a similar warning, and it concerned not what a person does but why. A good act performed for an audience, he suggests, may no longer be a good act at all.

Be careful, he said, not to practise your righteousness in front of others in order to be seen by them. If you do, then there is no reward for you from your Father in heaven. The sentence sets a test that every religious person must apply to their own motives, namely to whom the action is really addressed.

When you give to the poor, he continued, do not sound a trumpet in front of you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets to win the praise of men. Scholars debate whether this describes a real custom or is simply a humorous exaggeration, but the meaning does not depend on the answer. Anyone who has watched a donor wait for thanks knows exactly what Jesus describes.

The word hypocrite comes from the Greek for an actor, a person who plays a part on a stage and wears a mask. Those who give in order to be admired, Jesus said, have received their reward in full, and the reward is nothing more than the applause that they were seeking. They have been paid already, and so nothing further is owed to them by God, who is not impressed by display.

But when you give, he went on, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing. The picture is almost comic, as though a person were keeping a secret from one half of himself, and it means that giving should be so natural and quiet that one hardly takes notice of it. Generosity, in other words, should never be followed by self-congratulation or a wish to be thanked.

Giving to the poor was one of the most important duties of the Jewish faith, and the Law repeatedly told the people to care for the needy among them, for the widow, the orphan and the stranger. Jesus did not change this in any way, nor did he make it less important. What he asked was that it should be done with a pure heart and free from any desire for praise.

Your giving should be in secret, Jesus said, and your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you. He does not say what the reward will be, or when it will come, and the omission seems deliberate. It is left in God's hands, as something to trust and not to calculate.

Jesus then spoke about prayer, which was the second of the three practices of devotion that he had named. When you pray, he said, do not be like the hypocrites, who love to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the street corners so that everyone can see them. It is not that public prayer is wrong, but that prayer which is aimed at spectators has already lost its way.

When you pray, go into your room and close the door, and pray to your Father who is unseen. The word translated room can also mean a storeroom or an inner chamber, a private corner in a crowded house, and such a place was a natural refuge. Prayer, the saying suggests, is not a performance but a quiet and honest conversation between a person and God.

Jesus also warned against heaping up empty phrases, as people do who suppose that they will be heard for their many words. Your Father knows what you need before you ask him, he said, and so prayer need not be long or grand or full of clever speech. It can be simple and truthful, and that, in the end, is all that God asks of the one who prays.

“Pray then in this way,” said Jesus, and he gave his followers a short prayer that has since become the best-known prayer in the world. It has only a few lines, and it can be said in less than a minute, yet generations of Christians have found it inexhaustible. It is often called the Lord's Prayer, or the Our Father, and it is one of the first things that many Christian children learn.

The prayer opens with the words “Our Father in heaven,” and the choice of the word our is significant, since it joins everyone who prays it into a single family. Jesus invites his followers to approach God not as a distant ruler but as a loving parent, with both trust and respect. The first line therefore teaches that no one prays alone, even in the most private room.

The first request is that God's name be hallowed, which means kept holy and treated as something precious. In the ancient world a name stood for the whole character of a person, so the request is that God's character should be honoured and understood. It is a prayer that begins by looking up, and only afterwards looks at our own needs.

Next comes the plea that God's kingdom should come and his will be done on earth as it is in heaven. The one who prays is hoping for a world in which goodness and justice are not only ideals but realities, and is offering to take part in making it so. The prayer therefore joins the highest hope with the humblest everyday duty, and it asks the one who prays to be ready to act.

Then comes a plain and modest request, which is to give us today our daily bread. Bread was the staple food of the poor, and the plea is for what is needed for a single day, not for a store of riches or for years of safety. The Greek word for daily appears almost nowhere else, and translators have long debated its exact sense.

The prayer continues, “Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors,” and here the wording varies between versions of the prayer, some saying trespasses or sins in place of debts. All of them tie the forgiveness we receive from God to the forgiveness that we give to others. It is a bond that Jesus underlines in the very next verses of the sermon.

The final requests are for protection: do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil. The last word can also be translated the evil one, and the whole line asks for help in the trials that every person must face. It is a humble acknowledgement that we are not able to keep ourselves safe by our own strength alone.

Many churches close the prayer with the words, “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory for ever,” though the line is missing from the oldest copies of Matthew's Gospel. Scholars think that it was added by later copyists, probably because it was already used in worship, and it makes a fitting conclusion. Different churches therefore end the prayer in slightly different ways, and many omit the line entirely.

Jesus then returned to one line of the prayer and explained it further in plain words. If you forgive others when they sin against you, he said, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others, neither will your Father forgive you. It is one of the hardest and most searching sayings in the sermon, and it has never been easy to apply.

For about two thousand years Christians have said the prayer, and today they say it in almost every language on earth, in cathedrals, in prisons, in hospitals and at quiet bedsides. The Gospel of Luke records a shorter version of the prayer, which is why churches use slightly different words. Across all these differences, the prayer remains a shared inheritance of Christians in every part of the world.

Fasting was the third of the practices that Jesus examined, and once again he warned against turning a private act into a public performance. When you fast, he said, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, who make their faces miserable so that everyone can see their hunger. The reward of such a show, he noted, is nothing more than the admiration that it brings.

To fast is to go without food for a period of time, and in Jewish life it had long been a way of showing sorrow, seeking forgiveness or turning toward God. Some people fasted on certain days of the year, and some at times of personal need or trouble. It was a respected discipline, and Jesus did not suggest that people should give it up.

Instead, he said, anoint your head with oil and wash your face, so that no one can tell that you are fasting except your Father, who sees what is done in secret. In that society people ordinarily oiled their hair and washed in the morning, and so to do this was simply to look ordinary. Nothing in your appearance should announce the sacrifice that you are making, for the discipline is meant to remain a matter between you and God.

Jesus then moved from the practice of devotion to the question of wealth, and he told his followers not to store up treasure on earth. It is a place, he said, where moths and rust destroy and thieves break in and steal. Anything that can be eaten by insects or taken in the night, he implies, is a poor thing to build a life around.

The picture would have been very real to every listener, since many Galilean houses were built of mud brick, and a thief could dig through a wall. Clothes, which were a store of wealth, could be ruined by moths, and grain could be spoiled by damp and by pests. Even the most careful householder, however diligent, could never be wholly secure against the slow decay of insects or the sudden visit of a thief.

Store up your treasure in heaven instead, Jesus said, where moth and rust do not destroy and thieves do not break in. He is speaking of what lasts, such as kindness, mercy, faithfulness and the good that we do for others. These are the possessions that no army, no thief and no passing misfortune can ever take away from the one who has gathered them.

Then Jesus gave a short reason that has become a proverb: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. It is a shrewd observation, since we tend to follow what we value, and our spending and our time show us what we really love. The sentence invites each listener to ask honestly where their heart is currently resting.

He continued with a new picture, saying that the eye is the lamp of the body. If your eye is healthy, he said, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. How great is that darkness, he added, if the light inside you has become dark!

Some scholars note that in the language of the time a good eye could describe a generous person, and a bad eye could describe a greedy or envious one. If that is what Jesus means here, then the saying follows naturally from the one about treasure, and it says that our attitude to money shapes the whole of our lives. Even if the meaning is different, the picture of inner light and darkness is clear.

Jesus then declared that no one can serve two masters, because he will either hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money, he said, and the word that he used for money was Mammon, an old word for wealth and property. The saying does not condemn work or the need to live, but warns against letting riches rule the heart.

Having spoken about treasure and masters, Jesus turned to a burden that weighs on nearly everyone, which is anxiety about the necessities of life. Therefore, he said, do not worry about your life, about what you will eat or drink, or about what you will wear. The Greek word translated worry is often understood to describe a divided, restless mind that is pulled in several directions at once.

For many of those on the hillside these were not idle fears but the real questions of the day. A bad harvest, an illness or a lost day's work could leave a family without bread, and the poor lived close to that edge. Is not life more than food, Jesus asked, and the body more than the clothes that cover it, so that a person's worth cannot be measured by a meal or a cloak?

He then drew their attention to the birds of the air, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns. And yet, he said, your heavenly Father feeds them, quietly and without fail, every day of the year. It was a lesson that cost nothing, for the birds were an ordinary sight over every field and village, and anyone with eyes to see could learn from them.

Are you not worth much more than they are, Jesus asked, since you are cared for by the same heavenly Father? His question is not a command to be idle, for the birds themselves must search for every seed, and the farmers of Galilee worked hard for their harvests. It is a call to trust that human effort is held within a larger care, so that work need not be driven by dread.

Can any of you, by all your anxious thinking, add even a single hour to the length of your life, Jesus asked? Some translations speak of a cubit added to a person's height, since the Greek word can mean either a span of time or a measure of length. Either way the point is plain, because worry is powerless to give us anything that we want and is very good at spoiling what we already have.

Why do you worry about clothes, Jesus asked, and his words moved from the birds in the sky to the flowers on the ground. Consider the wild flowers, he said, which neither toil nor spin, and yet they grow in the fields. In spring the hills of Galilee are covered with wild flowers, such as poppies and anemones, so the example lay at the feet of every listener.

Yet not even Solomon in all his splendour, Jesus said, was dressed as beautifully as one of these simple flowers. Solomon was remembered as the wealthiest and wisest of Israel's kings, famous for his palace, his throne and his fine robes. Jesus asks his listeners to picture the greatest luxury they could imagine, and then he says that a humble flower surpasses it.

If God so clothes the grass of the field, Jesus continued, which is alive today and thrown into the oven tomorrow, will he not much more clothe you? In Galilee, dry grass and wild plants were gathered as fuel for clay ovens, so the picture of a short life and a fiery end was easily understood. He ends the thought with a gentle rebuke, calling his hearers people of little faith, a phrase that points to trust that is real but still small.

Those who do not know God, Jesus said, run after all these things, making food and clothing the whole aim of life. Your heavenly Father knows that you need them, and the one who knows our needs is also the one who can be trusted to meet them. The text therefore asks for a change of focus rather than a pretence that food and clothing do not matter.

Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, Jesus urged, and all these other necessities will be granted to you as well. Place God's way of life at the centre, in other words, and the ordinary needs of the day will settle into their proper order around it. Do not be consumed by anxiety about tomorrow, he concluded, for tomorrow will look after itself, and each day carries sufficient trouble of its own.

Jesus moved next to a habit that most people practise without noticing, the judging of other people's faults. Do not judge, he said, or you too will be judged, and there is no one in the crowd who is exempt. Each person on the hillside could easily imagine a neighbour who deserved a harsh word, and Jesus was speaking to that very temptation.

For with the judgment you give, he continued, you will be judged, and with the measure you use, it will be measured to you. In the market a seller scooped grain into a cup or a basket, and every buyer wanted the measure to be generous and exact. The sentence turns that familiar scene into a rule of life, which says that the standard that we apply to others will come back upon ourselves.

The saying echoes the prayer that Jesus had taught his followers, in which we ask to be forgiven as we forgive others. Both passages bind together the mercy that we receive and the mercy that we are asked to show, so that the two cannot be separated. A person who is quick to condemn and slow to forgive can hardly expect to be treated with patience in return.

At this point it is important for the reader to see what Jesus is not saying, since the saying has often been misunderstood. He is warning against the harsh, proud and hypocritical kind of judging that looks down on other people, and he is not forbidding all careful thought about right and wrong. Later in the same sermon he tells his listeners to beware of false prophets and to recognise them by their fruit, which requires them to use their judgment.

Jesus then offered an image so vivid that it may well have made some of his listeners smile, and perhaps wince as well. Why do you look at the speck in your friend's eye, he asked, and fail to notice the log that is in your own eye? The speck is a tiny grain of dust or sawdust, and the contrast with the log is intended to be startling.

The Greek word for the large object is a beam, the kind of timber that supports a roof. Matthew's picture is deliberately absurd, for no one could walk about with a roof beam in his eye and still imagine that he could help a neighbour with a speck of dust. Matthew's Gospel also calls Jesus the carpenter's son, and the image has something of the workshop about it.

First take the log out of your own eye, Jesus said, and then you will see clearly enough to remove the speck from your friend's eye. The order matters, for a person who has dealt honestly with his own faults is gentler and wiser in correcting others. The aim is therefore not to leave a friend's difficulty alone, but to help in a way that is humble, honest and kind.

Then came a saying that readers find puzzling, in which Jesus told his listeners not to give what is holy to dogs, and not to throw their pearls before pigs. If they do, he warned, the animals may trample the pearls under their feet and then turn and attack the one who threw them. It is one of the most debated sentences in the whole sermon, and no single explanation has satisfied every reader.

To many Jewish listeners dogs and pigs were unclean animals, which were roaming scavengers rather than household pets, and a pearl was among the costliest of treasures. Some readers think the saying asks for wisdom about when and how to share what is precious, and others take it as a warning about those who mock holy things. Whatever the exact meaning, the saying balances the gentleness of the earlier verses with a reminder that care and discernment are also part of love.

Taken together, the sayings about judging call for a humble heart, one that sees its own failings before it sees the failings of others. This links the passage back to the first blessing, which was for the poor in spirit, who know how much they need God. A person who is truly aware of his own need is slow to condemn, quick to forgive and ready to help.

Jesus had told his followers not to worry, and now he showed them what to do with their needs. Rather than carrying them alone and in silence, they were invited to bring them to God with a child's confidence. A few of the best-loved sayings in the whole sermon now follow, and they speak of a God who answers.

Ask, and it will be given to you, Jesus said; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you. There is a rising urgency in the three commands, as the one who prays moves from asking in words to searching and then to knocking at a door. In the Greek the verbs are in a form that suggests continuing action, and so they are often translated, keep asking, keep seeking and keep knocking.

For everyone who asks receives, Jesus continued, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks the door will be opened. The promise is stated with great simplicity, and it paints a picture of a house in which the door is not locked against those who come in need. Jesus offers the assurance as a statement about the character of God, and not as a formula for obtaining whatever a person might happen to wish.

To make the promise believable, Jesus turned to the ordinary experience of family life, which every listener had known as a child or as a parent. Which of you, he asked, if your son asks you for a loaf of bread, would hand him a stone instead? Every parent in the crowd knew the answer at once, and the very idea was absurd, since no loving father would mock his child's hunger.

Or if he asks for a fish, Jesus went on, will you give him a snake that might bite him as he reaches for it? Bread and fish were the common food of the lakeside villages, and a flat round stone could look rather like a small loaf. In each case the child asks for something good and plain, and in neither case would a decent parent answer with something useless or dangerous.

If you, who are far from perfect, know how to give good gifts to your children, Jesus said, how much more will your Father in heaven give good gifts to those who ask him? The Greek word is stronger than far from perfect, since it means evil, but the point of the comparison is not to condemn parents. It is to say that if flawed human love gives so freely, the love of God must be greater still.

Then Jesus drew this part of his teaching to a close with a sentence that is among the best known in the world. So in everything, he said, do to others whatever you would wish them to do to you, which turns our own desires into a measure for our conduct. The words follow from the picture of the generous Father, since those who have received good things are asked to share them.

For this, Jesus said, is the Law and the Prophets, which means that the saying sums up the teaching of all the holy writings of his people. Because it is so brief and so clear, it has long been called the Golden Rule, and it has been repeated in homes and schools for centuries. Its simplicity is its strength, though a person may spend a whole lifetime trying to live it faithfully.

Sayings of this kind are found in many traditions around the world, and they show how widely the idea has been shared. The Chinese teacher Confucius, who lived about five hundred years before Jesus, taught that one should not do to others what one does not want done to oneself. A Jewish teacher named Hillel, who lived shortly before Jesus, is remembered for a similar saying, and many of these are worded as warnings, whereas Jesus puts the rule as an action to take.

The positive form of the rule asks us to act for others, and not only to avoid harming them. It is not enough to keep our hands clean if we pass a hungry neighbour and leave him with nothing, for the rule calls for kindness that takes the first step. In this way the saying gathers up much of the sermon, which has taught mercy, gentleness, peacemaking and generosity from its opening blessings.

As the sermon neared its end, Jesus used a series of sharp pictures to ask his listeners for a decision. Enter through the narrow gate, he said, for wide is the gate and easy is the road that leads to destruction. The listeners were being invited to think of their lives as a journey, and every journey begins with going through some gate.

Many people, Jesus said, go in by that wide gate, and many travel along that easy road together. A broad road invites a crowd because it asks for no special effort and it is comfortable to walk with others who are going the same way. The warning is that popularity is no proof of wisdom, and that the easiest course may not be the one that leads to life.

But the gate that leads to life is narrow, he said, and the road is hard, and only a few find it. A narrow path demands care and attention, since a traveller must watch every step and cannot walk it carelessly. The picture suggests that a life of real goodness is not stumbled upon by accident but is found by those who are looking for it.

The picture of two ways would have been familiar to everyone on the hillside, since it runs through the holy writings of their own people. The first Psalm speaks of the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked, and Moses had set before Israel a choice between life and death. Jesus stands in that tradition, and he places the choice before his listeners in terms of how they respond to his own words.

The choice is a real one, and it is presented not to a chosen few but to every listener on the hillside. When Jesus says that few find the narrow gate, he does not tell us who they are, and readers should be careful about guessing which people are on which road. Since the sermon has just warned against judging, it would be strange to use this picture as a weapon against others.

Beware of false prophets, Jesus said, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. A prophet is one who speaks on behalf of God, and a false prophet is a teacher who claims that authority without possessing it. The picture is of a predator who has disguised himself as one of the flock, so that the danger lies precisely in how harmless he looks.

If the wolves look so much like sheep, how can anyone tell the difference between the false and the true? You will know them by their fruit, Jesus answered, and the answer is as plain as the harvest in an orchard. Fruit is what a life produces, and it can be seen by anyone willing to look patiently at what a person does over time.

Do people gather grapes from thorn bushes, Jesus asked, or figs from thistles, and expect a good harvest? Grapes and figs were two of the best-known fruits of the land, and every farmer and village child knew that a thorny plant could produce neither. The rule of the garden is the rule of life, for each plant yields only the fruit of its own kind.

In the same way, he said, every good tree bears good fruit, and a bad tree bears bad fruit. A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot bear good fruit, and any tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. The saying is a plain warning, for it shows that an outward show of religion cannot hide, for long, what a person really is.

By their fruit you will recognise them, Jesus said again, so the test is not what a person claims but what a person produces. The fruit of a life is its honesty, mercy, patience and courage, as these show themselves in ordinary days, and they cannot be faked forever. This test has the advantage of being open to all, for anyone may look at it, and the first person to examine should be oneself.

Jesus now gave a solemn warning about the gap that can open between what people say and what they do. Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, he said, will enter the kingdom of heaven, however warmly the title is spoken. Honouring Jesus with the right title is not enough by itself if the life that follows does not match the words.

Only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven, Jesus said, will enter that kingdom. The weight of the sentence falls on the word doing, since the sermon has been full of commands about mercy, honesty, forgiveness and peace, and these are meant to be practised. It is a reminder that a life of faith is measured as much by conduct as by speech.

Jesus pictured a future day of reckoning on which many people would come forward, each ready to plead a case. On that day, he said, many will say to me, Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and drive out demons in your name, and do many wonders in your name? The list is impressive, and it is made up of the very acts that a community would be proud to see.

Then I will tell them plainly, Jesus said, I never knew you, and the words come as a shock after so long a list of good deeds. Christians have read these sobering words in different ways, some stressing the warning against empty religion and others the mystery of who is finally known to God. Many readers feel that the saying is meant to wake the hearer to what matters most, and not to leave anyone paralysed by fear.

Words, titles and even impressive deeds are therefore no substitute for a life of obedience from the heart. A person may speak well, hold a high place and do remarkable things, and yet lack the plain goodness that Jesus asks for. What matters most, the sermon suggests, is a heart that listens carefully and then acts upon what it has heard.

Jesus closed the sermon with a short story about two builders, and its meaning is easy to remember. Everyone who hears these words of mine and acts on them, he said, is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. The wise builder chose firm ground before he set the first stone, and it was careful work that nobody would see once the house was finished.

The rain fell, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, as they would against any other. Yet it did not fall, Jesus said, because its foundation was on the rock, and the strength of the house lay in what was hidden beneath it. The storm is not meant as a rare disaster but as a picture of testing, and the story assumes that sooner or later every life will meet one.

In Galilee a dry stream bed could fill with astonishing speed after heavy rain, so that a quiet valley became a rushing torrent in a short time. Anyone who had lived through the winter rains in that land would have understood the picture at once and felt its force. A house built beside such a stream needed firm foundations, or the first great storm would wash it away.

Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not act on them, Jesus said, is like a foolish man who built his house on sand. Sand can look like perfectly good ground in dry weather, and the foolish builder may have saved time and labour by building on it. The difference between the two houses could not be seen on a sunny day, and it appeared only when the storm arrived.

Then the same storm arrived, with the same rain, the same floods and the same winds, and it beat against the second house. It fell, and great was its fall, and the ruin of the second house was as complete as the safety of the first had been. The story ends on that stark note, leaving each listener to decide which kind of builder to be.

When Jesus had finished saying these things, Matthew tells us, the crowds who had listened were amazed at his teaching. With this short sentence the Gospel turns from the sermon itself to the effect that it had on its hearers. The writer does not describe what they did next, but he leaves the impression of people who had heard something that they could not forget.

They were astonished, Matthew says, because he taught them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes. The word translated authority describes a power to speak with the right to be heard, and it is a word that Matthew uses of Jesus several times. The crowd sensed that this teacher was not repeating a lesson learned from others but speaking from some source of his own.

Scribes in those days usually supported their words by quoting the opinions of earlier teachers, and a good teacher showed that he belonged to a chain of respected voices. Jesus did something different, for he said in each of the six sayings, I say to you, and he spoke as if the words came from himself. This confidence is one reason why the crowd was so astonished, and it has led readers ever since to ask who this teacher was.

Matthew's Gospel arranges much of the teaching of Jesus into five great sections, and the Sermon on the Mount is the first and the best known. Each section ends with a similar phrase, such as when Jesus had finished saying these things, which marks the close of a speech and the return to the story. Many scholars think that the pattern was deliberate, and some suggest that the five sections were meant to recall the five books of the Law of Moses.

Some readers see Jesus as a new Moses, who gives teaching from a mountain just as Moses brought the Law down from Mount Sinai. Matthew's opening chapters encourage the comparison, since the infant Jesus is saved from a cruel king, as Moses was, and is later called out of Egypt. Others read the scene more simply, as a teacher who goes up a hillside so that a crowd can see and hear him, and the question remains open.

In brief, the sermon has spoken of blessings, salt and light, a deeper law, secret devotion, trust in the Father, gentleness toward others and the building of a life on firm ground. It is a long teaching, and a reader may find it helpful to hold it in the mind as a single journey. Each theme returns to the same question, which is what kind of person a listener hopes to become.

Matthew says that when Jesus saw the crowds, he went up on the mountainside, and his disciples came to him and he began to teach them. The crowd, however, was listening too, and by the end of the sermon Matthew writes that the crowds were amazed. Readers therefore ask who the sermon was really for, and some say the disciples, others the crowd, and many that it was meant for anyone who would listen.

Christian tradition says that Matthew, once a tax collector, wrote this Gospel, although scholars debate who the writer was. Whoever he was, he was writing for early Christians, probably many of them Jewish, and he wanted them to remember what Jesus taught. The sermon was therefore preserved as a guide for a community that was trying to live by it.

Above the Sea of Galilee, near Capernaum, stands a church called the Church of the Beatitudes, which marks the traditional site of the sermon. Pilgrims have long climbed the hillside to sit and read the words there, looking out over the water. In truth no one knows the exact spot, and the Gospel says only that Jesus went up a mountainside.

The pictures of the sermon were so plain that ordinary listeners could remember them without any written text. A fisherman or a farmer could repeat the saying about the salt, the lamp or the house on the rock to his family at home in the evening. In this way the teaching may have travelled from village to village on the lips of those who had heard it, long before anyone copied it onto a scroll.

Luke's Gospel contains a shorter teaching that begins with blessings and sets them beside warnings, and it is set not on a mountainside but on a level place. Luke has four blessings and four matching warnings, and he includes other sayings that Matthew also gives, such as love of enemies and the golden rule. Many readers call the passage the Sermon on the Plain, and they compare it with Matthew's version to see what each writer wanted to say.

Believers and scholars explain the differences between the two versions in several ways, and the discussion is a long and lively one. Some say that Jesus taught the same things many times in different places, so that Matthew and Luke each recorded a different occasion. Others think that the two writers gathered sayings from earlier collections and shaped them to suit their own readers, and they hold that this does not lessen their value.

A very early Christian writing called the Didache, which probably dates from within about a century of the time of Jesus, makes use of the sermon's teaching. It tells its readers to bless those who curse them, to pray for their enemies, to turn the other cheek and to give to everyone who asks. The sermon was therefore being read and put to use by Christians very early, as a guide for daily conduct.

In about the year 394, Augustine, a church leader in North Africa, wrote a long commentary on the sermon. He treated it as a map of the Christian life, leading the reader step by step from the first blessing to the house built on rock. His book has been read for more than sixteen hundred years, and it shows that the sermon was already being studied closely in the fourth century.

In the early 1530s Martin Luther, the German reformer, preached through the whole sermon to the people of his town. He insisted that its teaching was meant for ordinary Christians in every walk of life, and not only for monks or for a spiritual elite who had left the world behind. For Luther the farmer, the mother and the magistrate were all called to live out the sermon in the place where they stood.

In the 1800s the Russian novelist Leo Tolstoy came to see the sermon as the heart of the teaching of Jesus. He read it as a command to non-violence and a refusal to answer evil with force, and he wrote about this in a famous book called The Kingdom of God Is Within You. His ideas upset both state and church, but they spread far beyond Russia and reached a young lawyer in South Africa.

Mohandas Gandhi, who was a Hindu, wrote that the Sermon on the Mount went straight to his heart. He was especially moved by the sayings about turning the other cheek and loving enemies, and he drew on them, with other sources, in his campaigns of non-violent protest in South Africa and India. To Gandhi the sermon suggested that the highest teaching could be lived out in public life, and not only admired from a distance.

In 1957 Martin Luther King, a Baptist pastor in Montgomery, Alabama, preached a sermon called Loving Your Enemies, which was based on the words of Jesus in this sermon. He taught that love, and not hatred or revenge, must guide the struggle for civil rights, and that hatred damages the one who hates as well as the one who is hated. He preached it at a time when he and his followers were facing threats and violence, which gave his words a particular weight.

In 1937 the German pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer published a book about the sermon, called The Cost of Discipleship. He warned against what he called cheap grace, which is forgiveness offered without any change of life, and he argued that real grace calls a person to follow Jesus in action. Bonhoeffer wrote as the Nazis held power in Germany, and he was later put to death for his part in the resistance, so his words carried the weight of his own life.

Some Jewish readers admire the sermon and read it as part of the Jewish tradition of teaching, since many of its sayings echo the Law, the Prophets and the wisdom of the rabbis. They may still differ with Christians about who Jesus was, and the sermon has become a place where readers of both faiths can meet, study and learn from one another. Scholars on all sides also warn that the sermon's remarks about scribes and Pharisees must never be used as a weapon against Jewish people today.

The hard sayings of the sermon, such as turn the other cheek, love your enemies and tear out your eye, have been read in several different ways over the centuries. Christians do not all understand them alike, and it helps a reader to know which view belongs to which tradition. Several of the main readings are set out here fairly, so that each can be understood on its own terms.

Some groups, such as the Mennonites and the Quakers, try to follow the sermon quite literally, and its commands have shaped their way of life. They have often refused to fight in wars and to swear oaths, taking seriously the sayings about not resisting an evildoer and not swearing at all. For them the sermon is a plain description of how a follower of Jesus is meant to live, and they have sometimes paid a price for their convictions.

Others, including many Lutherans, say that the sermon shows how far we fall short of God's way, however sincerely we try. In their view the commands are so high that no one can keep them perfectly, and this discovery drives a person to trust in God's grace and not in his own goodness. The sermon then acts as a mirror, which reveals our need, and not as a ladder, which we are meant to climb by our own effort.

Many other readers take the sermon as a direction for the heart and for character, and not as a set of rules to be applied one by one. On this view Jesus uses vivid and even extreme pictures to show the spirit in which a person should live, and his hearers were meant to be moved and challenged by them. The sermon then describes the kind of person that a follower of Jesus is called to become, and it leaves each reader to work out what that means in daily life.

Albert Schweitzer, a scholar who wrote in the early 1900s, argued that Jesus expected God's kingdom to arrive very soon. On this view Jesus taught for a short and extraordinary time, and his commands were meant for that brief period before the end, so that they were not a plan for ordinary generations. Many scholars dispute this reading, but it has had a lasting influence, and it reminds us that the sermon was first spoken in a particular world and a particular time.

The sermon moves from who we are, in the blessings, to what we do, in the sayings about law, devotion, trust and relationships. It ends with a call to act, in the story of the two builders, so that the whole teaching has a clear shape from the first word to the last. A reader who follows that movement sees that character comes first and that conduct grows from it, as fruit grows from a tree.

The pictures of the sermon come from the everyday world of Galilee, from salt and lamps, birds and wild flowers, gates and houses on rock or sand. These were things that every listener could see and touch, so the teaching did not need to be explained, and it could be carried home and recalled in the course of an ordinary day. That may be one reason why it has travelled so far and lasted so long, for anyone in any country can find a lamp, a bird or a house in his own life.

The sermon opens with blessing for the poor, the gentle, the merciful and the peacemakers before it gives any command at all. Many readers see this as the key to the whole, since it suggests that people are welcomed and valued before they are asked to change. The commands that follow can then be heard as an invitation to live in the light of that welcome, and not as a price to be paid for it.

Readers of every background, believers or not, have taken the sermon as a question about what kind of person to be. Some come to it as an act of faith, some as a work of literature and some as a challenge to their own habits, and each finds something that speaks to their own time. Whatever the reader's belief, the pictures and sayings invite each one to think about mercy, honesty, peace and trust, and to ask what a good life really requires.

When Jesus came down from the mountainside, Matthew writes, large crowds followed him, and the long teaching was over. Its words have been read, argued over and loved for about two thousand years, by those who call themselves his followers and by many who do not. The hillside above the lake is quiet now, but the questions that Jesus raised there are still asked by anyone who wants to learn how to live.
